speechtext: I want to take a moment of the time of the house, Mr. Speaker. There are a lot of questions we would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), but we can ask them another time. There is one question I should like to put to the minister and it is this. Was it generally foreseen that because of the terms of what I believe was called the uniting for peace resolution, which was passed about a year ago by the United Nations general assembly, that the resolutions passed at the United Nations general assembly on November 2 and November 7 last, which were based on the former resolution would be clearly placing the Egyptian president in a position to dictate to the United Nations with respect to the emergency force?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps I could just try to answer that in a word. When the uniting for peace resolution was passed by the assembly, as my hon. friend may know, two committees were set up by the assembly to follow up the question of uniting for peace through the appropriate machinery. Canada was represented on one of those committees. At that time we did try to make provision, and made proposals to that effect, for some permanent United Nations police machinery which would be available for the kind of emergency which took place last October. This was not possible and, therefore, though we may have at that time foreseen the kind of emergency which we had at the end of last October, I am afraid we did not do very much to be in a position to meet it.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before making the remarks which I propose to make I should like to associate myself with those who have congratulated the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think this is more than just a pleasant piece of politeness. I believe it indicates something which is quite basic in our parliamentary practice and which has been referred to in these 
very often quoted words of Churchill who said, "The things that unite us are greater than the things that divide". Also, I think it is part and parcel of another thing which is essential in our parliamentary life, namely, a kind of sense of sportsmanship which does not often desert us, and which, when it does desert us, causes difficulties. I think ordinarily we have the feeling that, as I said, we can afford to be polite to each other, usually, because of the fact that the things that unite are greater than the things that divide.
I had no idea when I put together my thoughts to express today that I should have the honour of following the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I had, in fact, determined to base my remarks on that paragraph in the speech from the throne which did have a passing reference to the commonwealth and I do not propose to be diverted from that except that I shall try to comment on some of the remarks made by the minister with particular reference to the commonwealth.
I want to read the paragraph which refers to the commonwealth:
Visits to Canada in the last few weeks by the prime ministers of Ceylon and India have been conducive to a renewed strengthening of the bonds which unite the peoples of the commonwealth in their constant aim to co-operate in the pursuit of peace, liberty and progress.
Now, I suppose I ought to be grateful for two reasons that Mr. Nehru and the prime minister of Ceylon were here; if they had not been here we might not have had any reference to the commonwealth at all in the speech from the throne; and it is interesting to have them here, too, because of the fact that in the case of Nehru he represents hundreds of millions of Asians. We are reminded of this fact incidentally, in the article by the Right Hon. Mr. Nutting in the Montreal Gazette when he pointed out the other day that our great task now is to make friends with the teeming millions in what he called the "uncommitted world".
I find the words I have read from the speech from the throne very disappointing. There is nothing in them which suggests any action, and that is my criticism of the pleasant words used by the minister this morning in speaking about the commonwealth. "The visit is conducive to a renewed strengthening of the bonds". There is not very much suggestion of action there.
I suppose something had to be said about the commonwealth because of what happened in this chamber last November. A great many of us remember with great regret the words

used by the Prime Minister on November 26 when he said, as reported at page 20 of Hansard:
The era when the supermen of Europe could govern the whole world has and is coming pretty close to an end.
We remember not only the caustic words but the caustic tone which he used, and perhaps it was not surprising that before the session ended on November 29 the Prime Minister thought it wise to temper those caustic words in what I can only call a speech of repentance. It seems to me repentance; I think it was repentance. I quote briefly from the Prime Minister's words at page 174 of Hansard:
While I am on my feet there was something I did wish to say, which I think was expressed in some of the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops and other hon. members and is summarized in a paragraph of an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of today. It reads:
"Canada should have but one major goal for its foreign policy these days, more important even than the doings of its troops in Egypt: that is the immediate improvement of commonwealth relations, of Anglo-American-French relations-but the greatest need of all is the reuniting of the principles and policies of the British and American governments".
That is the end of the quotation from the Journal. The Prime Minister goes on:
I had intended to take the opportunity of saying that had been the goal we have been pursuing ever since the first of these resolutions came before the United Nations, to work toward what we regard as almost essential for the peace and security of the free world; that is to say, the reliance on commonwealth relations and the reuniting of this alliance in an effective way between the United Kingdom, France and the United States; something that has, I think, been of immense value and without which there would be a void that would cause all of us deep anxiety.
In these words of the Prime Minister there was some warmth, some suggestion of action, but when we come again to read these tepid, lukewarm words in the speech from the throne there is no suggestion of warmth or of action. It is, as I say, a tepid, lukewarm performance.
I do not propose to refer at any great length to the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. One might say of it "good sentences, and well pronounced," in his reference to the commonwealth. I do not feel that I can quarrel much with what he said; they were fair words. But what one wants to know is what is going to be done. Is there any sign of action? And, also, I cannot rid myself entirely of the wonder whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs is so completely North American, is so completely engrossed with his dealings with Washington, that he finds it impossible to take very seriously the affairs of the commonwealth. We remember when, some years
The Address-Mr. Macdonnell ago, he came back from a meeting at Colombo with the other commonwealth nations and announced that he had been there as a "dollar gadfly." A gadfly is a not very co-operative form of insect. I understand what he meant, of course, is that he had been there, the only member representing a country not in the sterling bloc, and that he had been at pains to outline the special views of Canada as a non-member of the sterling bloc.
I wish to refer just briefly to another matter which troubles and perplexes me because of the fair words the minister uses about the commonwealth. He delivered some lectures at Princeton a year or more ago and I intend to read from page 95 of this book of lectures. I am also going to refer to an editorial reviewing the book in the Queen's University Quarterly. The reviewer says in brief:
One very puzzling aspect of Mr. Pearson's . . . discussion is that there is only one mention of the commonwealth of nations.
That is, in this whole book of 120 pages or so. The reviewer goes on to say that while there are frequent references to the Atlantic triangle and our allies as represented by the Atlantic triangle there is only this one reference to the commonwealth of nations. As a matter of fact, the reference is introduced in rather curious words, almost words of apology. This was originally delivered as a lecture at Princeton University and I am now quoting from page 95 of the book of lectures:
Before leaving this subject of understanding between systems of society and civilizations, I would like to mention-and it can be only to mention- the unique role which may be played in this matter by the commonwealth of nations of which Canada is privileged to be a member. Its value as a bridge of understanding between the west and Asia and Africa is very great in this age of suspicion and strain where there are few such bridges.
Well, I do not quarrel with those words; indeed, I rather welcome them. I would go back again to ask, however, whether we find any evidence of action as described in these fair words and in particular whether this paragraph which I have read suggests action or any approach to action. I find myself disappointed and indeed there are other things too which disappoint me. If we think back to the time when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) returned from the commonwealth conference last summer we will recall that he had very little to say about what had taken place. He said they had not had to deal at any length with the affairs of the commonwealth itself because they did not

The Address-Mr. Macdonnell really need attention. His exact words as reported at page 5764 of Hansard for July 9, 1956 were:
Problems of the commonwealth, as such, did not require very much attention.
It is quite true that the conference had discussed various other matters but we could get very little satisfaction from the Prime Minister because, as he said, "The problems of the commonwealth, as such, did not require very much attention". Those were the words of the Prime Minister on his return on July 9 last and when the then leader of the opposition, and the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) too, asked whether there was any indication of our taking the initiative in calling a future meeting the answer was in the negative.
In view of what has happened in these last few months I think the question arises again as to whether we can take the lead. If times were normal one could better tolerate a passive attitude, but the times are not normal. In the morning paper we read a remark of Mr. Chou En-lai of China who has been hailing the Russians as the leaders of the communists in the world and referring to the rest of us as "the enemy". I think the question arises as to whether we do or do not take these things seriously. If we do not, that is that; but if we do, then I suggest again that no proper steps are being taken to give the commonwealth the scope which it might have.
I wish to refer to Mr. Nutting's words in Saturday's Gazette in which he refers to the Anglo-American bridge. There are all kinds of bridges being referred to these days. He said:
First I want to set forth some general ideas on the basic problems that face our two countries.
Our survival depends on whether we can make friends not with communism but with the millions of the uncommitted world. That is the simple life and death issue which faces us, how do we approach it?
I come back to the paragraph I read from the speech from the throne and ask whether it means anything at all. Do the fair words of the minister this morning mean anything at all? Do they indicate any function for the commonwealth or do they just give it a blessing? Do we regard ourselves merely as members of a club or are we members of a live organization that is able to play its part?
The commonwealth has a special role among free nations and I want to read a sentence from an extremely interesting lecture delivered not long ago in Britain by Sir Oliver Franks, who has this to say about the commonwealth. Franks, you will remember, was the British Ambassador in Washington for

some years and he gives rather an amusing picture of his arrival in these words:
The nations of the commonwealth are free and equal: they are all sovereign states. This was impressed on me the very first day I arrived in Washington. There was a group at the station to welcome me. It included the chief of protocol from the American State Department, British Embassy staff, and seven commonwealth ambassadors. I suddenly realized that there were already six representatives of His Majesty in Washington, as well as the Indian ambassador whose government recognized the King as head of the commonwealth. From one point of view, and it was a real one, I was the junior ambassador of His Majesty in the United States.
At page 21 he says:
The strength and vitality of the commonwealth does not lie in the separation of its members from their neighbours. It is not that sort of exclusive club. It is its nature to reach out, not to retreat like a snail into its shell. Rightly conceived, the connections of interest and policy which each commonwealth nation enjoys with its neighbours are a source of strength to the whole, not of weakness. They contribute to the effective working of the commonwealth because they increase the understanding and the influence of each member in its region. And between them the members cover five continents of the world.
Its members, one might say, have a dual role. Australia and New Zealand are part of Southeast Asia and they are also part of the commonwealth. Canada is part of the commonwealth but is also part of North America. Britain is part of the commonwealth and also part of Europe. India, Ceylon and Pakistan are part of Asia and also part of the commonwealth, and today we were told of other eastern nations that will shortly be coming into the commonwealth as well. We remind ourselves that in addition to the commonwealth there is NATO about which we hear so much and there is also ANZUS; that is the Pacific organization comprising Australia, New Zealand and the United States. It is still in existence and it continues to function although we do not hear nearly so much about it as we hear about NATO.
Having another look at the commonwealth we observe it is not a bloc. It is spread all over the world separated by large tracts of sea. As someone has said so aptly, "By its very existence it says to the world, 'Don't just be American or European or Asian or African, but something more than that. Be worldwide.' " It has something more in common than the sharing of a continent and it can bring the continents together.
I wish to read at greater length from what the minister said in his Princeton lecture. At page 95 the following words appear:
I would like to mention the unique role which may be played in this matter by the commonwealth of nations .	.	. This is a loose but intimate
association which includes in its membership nations from each of the continents. Its value as

a bridge of understanding between the west and Asia and Africa is very great in this age of suspicion and strain where there are few such bridges .	. . The strength of the commonwealth
lies precisely in the undefined but genuine recognition by its members of the value to each of such an association with the others and of a common interest in the preservation of a system which includes us all.
I repeat that these are fine sentiments and are well expressed but the question which continually arises in my mind is that of action. Now the circumstances of the moment of course, in view of what has happened during these last months, suggest more than ever the strengthening of the commonwealth. Let us be frank. Britain has taken a knock, but do not let us forget 1940. A lot of people were ready to write her off then but we all remember the magnificent recovery which was made and I believe it will happen again. I do not think those 50 million brave and able people are going to play any second-rate part in world affairs. Their country is not as big or strong as the United States, of course, but I do not think they can be relegated to any second-rate role.
I have been discussing, particularly, political considerations up to now and those were the only considerations which the minister (Mr. Pearson) discussed this morning. That is one of the things that disappointed me-he said nothing about anything specific; he gave no indication of any function which the commonwealth could exercise at the moment; and yet it seems to me, there is a matter of vast importance spread before our eyes now and that is the question of whether Britain is going to join a free trade bloc of nations in Europe. Speaking of this possibility the Winnipeg Free Press says:
This is a bold design, if it is ever effectively translated into practice-through a transition period of perhaps ten years and more-It will recast the structure of world trade.
I am amazed that the minister said nothing about that this morning. I would have thought he should be particularly alive and alert to that situation. But there is no word, as far as I know, of any commonwealth conference being held this year, as has been requested. I can only hope it will take place this year because it seems to me it has now got something important to get its teeth into.
I am going to read a short piece from the London Economist's Canadian representative because he has things to say about this free trade prospect that I think we should bear in mind:
Canada must be concerned and disappointed that the free trade area as now envisaged by the British government puts paid to all hopes of expanding the exports of Canadian manufacturers to Britain. It is not comforting to hear British ministers brush
The Address-Mr. Macdonnell off-as Mr. Macmillan has done-the "mere ten per cent" of present Canadian exports which would be affected by the plan.
It is true our manufactured exports are only ten per cent. Then the correspondent goes on to say this:
Most of the ten per cent consists of semi-fabricated goods like paper of various kinds, chemicals- whenever import licences could be obtained-and some synthetic fibres. All of them benefit from substantial preferences. If the quota restrictions can be overcome, the tariff has been favourable. All these commodities represent the fractional beginnings of what Canada has always hoped might develop into considerable lines of trade.
Later the article goes on to say:
Some of the most important products concerned, moreover, have been things like chemicals where Canada is establishing new domestic industries to which even a limited export market was of great importance. When therefore Canada is invited to give up all preference on its manufactured goods as against Europe, the reluctance stemmed chiefly not from attachment to the present ten per cent of exports but rather from the shattered dream of the exports that might have been.
Those are serious words used by serious men and yet no reference of any kind has been made to them today by the minister. It is quite true, when facing this situation that we must remember that Canada would have a special problem in any negotiations because of her status as a dollar country, but that does not mean the problem should be ignored; it merely means that it is a challenge to statesmanship.
If we lose vital contacts with the commonwealth we shall fall more and more into the orbit of the United States and increasingly lose our individuality; we are finding out what that means to an ever-increasing degree.
I have tried to make a case on the political side and in practical matters of trade. If the case is as strong as I have indicated, why are we not more forthcoming? I think there are two reasons, among others. I sometimes wonder if we are as forthcoming as Australia and New Zealand. I do not think we are. First, for example, I noted that the minister of external affairs in his book containing the Princeton lectures had occasion only once, in those lectures, to mention the commonwealth and even then rather apologetically. Is it because we are so dominated by the U.S.? Then there is, apparently, another reason which I mention particularly because I think it is so wrong, and that is the feeling that close association with the commonwealth will somehow lessen our position as an autonomous state. I think that is so wrong, and yet it presents the danger of driving a wedge between the two founding races in our country. Yet I believe that if we would consider it carefully we would find there is

The Address-Mr. Macdonnell nothing in this point at all. I wish in this connection to quote briefly from three of the great voices of the past who have spoken on this subject-Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden.
Sir John Macdonald, speaking on February 20, 1890, in this house in a speech which concerned the rights of the French language, said:
I appeal to all our friends In this house, without reference to party, to forget what may be an inconvenience when they go back to their constituents on both sides; to forget that for a moment, and to merge everything in the great desire to make Canada, French and English, one people without any hostile feeling, without any difference in feeling, further than that which arises from the different literatures and the different strains of mind that run always in different races and which sever the Scotsman and the Irishman from the Englishman as much as they sever the Frenchman from the Englishman. Let us forget this cry and we shall have our reward in seeing this unfortunate fire which has been kindled from so small a spark extinguished forever and we shall go on as we have been going on since 1867 as one people with one object, looking to one future and expecting to lay the foundations of one great country.
And now I wish to quote words from Sir Wilfrid Laurier which interested me particularly, partly because of the place in which they were uttered but also because of their intrinsic merit. When Sir Wilfrid was at the diamond jubilee in 1897 shortly after he became Prime Minister, he had occasion to visit Paris, and speaking in Paris he said this:
In passing through this city, beautiful beyond all cities, I have noticed upon many public buildings the proud device that the armies of the republic carried through Europe-Liberty, Equality and Fraternity. Very well: all that there is of worth, of greatness, of generosity in that device we have today in Canada, that is our conquest. We have liberty absolute, complete; more complete-pardon my national pride for the affirmation I am making -more complete than in any country whatsoever in the world. Liberty for our religion, liberty for our language-liberty for all the institutions which our ancestors brought from France and which we regard as a sacred heritage. Equality is ours. What other proof of it could I give you than this? In this country, where the majority is of English descent and of the Protestant religion, the last general election have brought to power a man of French descent and Catholic religion, who has always strongly affirmed his race and religion. Fraternity is ours. There is with us no domination of one race over another. . . .
If in becoming subjects of the British crown, we have been able to keep our ancient rights and even acquire new ones, upon the other hand we have undertaken obligations, which, descended as we are from a chivalrous race, we recognize in full and hold ourselves in honour bound to proclaim. .	.	. That double fidelity to ideas and
aspirations quite distinct, is our glory-Canada. We are faithful to the great nation which gave us life, we are faithful to the great nation which has given us liberty.
I quote briefly from Sir Robert Borden, who was quoted by the Prime Minister himself the other day at the ceremony in connection
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
with the unveiling of Sir Robert's statue. This is an extract from a speech given before the Canadian Bar Association in 1929:
On the whole there has been an honourable and wholesome co-operation of the two races in the upbuilding of Canadian institutions and in the development of the heritage with which Providence has endowed the Canadian nation. The pioneer races are and they always will be distinctive but in their origins they are much nearer to each other than either seems to imagine. It is desirable to emphasize their points of sympathy and contact rather than their divergences of temperament and outlook.
I have quoted these words; I have reminded the house of the decisive part which the commonwealth played in two wars. I have indicated the enormous potential importance of commonwealth influence. I have pointed out its widespread ramifications and its influence everywhere in the world. I have reminded you that notwithstanding the autonomy of its component parts it has always been able to act together in crises. I have emphasized the need of unity of heart and purpose at home. I have quoted the great voices of the past.
I come back again to the urgent hope, the urgent demand that somehow or other this commonwealth will be able to play a greater part. I believe we have been soft pedalling. I feel it has not done what it should. I feel that the proximity of Washington and our constant contact with urgent problems which may arise there have perhaps served as an excuse but not as a reason for soft pedalling the work which the commonwealth can do and the services it can render. I believe that the services it can render are perhaps greater than ever before.
We have been well described as constituting a bridge between the east and the west, but in a sense we are also a bridge between the United States and the United Kingdom. That gives us a dual role, but it should not lead us to soft pedal the one because the claims of the other can so easily become insistent. Surely this all adds up to the conclusion that we should not be content with these tepid half-hearted words. I do hope that we shall have an indication that the real intention of the government is not expressed by these words and that we shall have action which will be much more reassuring than those faint and stumbling words which I have read.
Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National
Health and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I believe that it is in accordance with our parliamentary traditions that one who has had the experience I have had in the last 63 days should at the first opportunity make a report to his colleagues in the House of Commons in a general way and through this house to the people at

large of an experience which has been certainly for me of great value, and which I would like to think will prove to be of value to the country and to the assignment I was asked to undertake. Without having had an opportunity of preparing the headings under which I propose to speak I hope on this account I shall not be less effective in giving the house some of the information and some of the impressions which I gathered during my trip to South and Southeast Asia.
I was asked by the Prime Minister and my colleagues in the government to represent Canada at the consultative meetings on the ministerial level of the Colombo plan which were held, beginning on December 4, in Wellington, New Zealand and at the same time to take advantage of that long journey to visit some 13 countries in South and Southeast Asia with which Canada has not had as great contact in the past as have many other nations whose history and period of existence is longer than our own.
So on November 11 I journeyed first to the Philippines and from there to Indo-China to Viet Nam, Cambodia and Laos. I am the first Canadian minister of the crown to have had the privilege of going to Indo-China at any time, certainly since the setting up of the three international supervisory commissions which operate in those three countries in that historic part of Asia. From there I went to Indonesia and then to Thailand; from there to Australia and to New Zealand for the Colombo plan meeting. Then back to Sydney, that great city in Australia, and on to Canberra for consultation and talks with the prime minister and members of the government of Australia.
Afterward I journeyed to Singapore, to Malaya, to Ceylon, to India and Pakistan, and then back home.
In all of these places I had the opportunity of discussing matters with the head of every state where the head of the state is actually the chief of government. In those countries where the prime minister is the head of the government or, as in the case of Singapore and Malaya where the chief minister is the head of the government, I had the opportunity of conferring and talking with these latter persons on matters of mutual and world interest. Likewise in every country I had the opportunity of valuable talks with all the foreign ministers but one and with my opposite numbers in the field of health and welfare. I should like now to thank all of those governments for the opportunities which they provided me as a member of the government of Canada to discuss with them problems of common interest and of international concern.
The Address-Mr. Martin
It is I know difficult to draw conclusions from what one has seen and heard. It is possible sometimes to formulate too readily impressions which one has gathered particularly in a continent like Asia with its millions of people, more people than are to be found anywhere else in the world, more in the two countries of China and India than in all Europe and all the Americas together. The overriding impression I gained is that in the formulation of policy which has to do with the peace of the world, with the relations of one state with another, we ought in the assessment we make of other peoples' conduct and actions, of other governments' policies, to seek to understand the circumstances and the context in which those policies are formulated and projected. That certainly is true of Asia.
Canada has consistently sought to express to all nations its friendship and understanding. It has not received in return the kind of collaboration and appreciation that one would sometimes think it should receive from certain quarters. But as between Canada and India, for instance, there has been, during the past half decade at any rate, a close understanding and a disposition on our part to appreciate the significant and potential role and actual role which that country can play in Asia and in international affairs generally.
In spite of that, and although I in a modest way at the United Nations have from time to time been part of this desire to understand India, I must frankly say that I did say in India on several occasions that some of the attitudes taken in Asia did cause me personally at any rate on occasion to express some wonderment. In the light of this, with existing foreshadowings in terms of geography that confront that great nation and other Asian nations, I can well understand how important it is that each of us, officially and privately, try to understand the problems immediately confronting some of these countries and at the same time urge that there be reciprocal action on their part as to the reasons we in the west on occasion take the courses which, in our interests and in the interests of the world at large, from our point of view we regard as essential.
I neglected to mention that among the countries I visited was Burma, which borders on China, close to Indo-China and India. It is a country of 18 millions of people dedicated to the principles of a strong religious belief. It serves as a symbol in one sense, of the kind of forces that are at play in that great land mass we call Asia.
Wherever I went I sought first of all to affirm our friendship for these nations, and

The Address-Mr. Martin to indicate to them that the Canadian government, regardless of party, and the Canadian people, disposed as they are toward building a peaceful world, had for them nothing but a desire of friendship and collaboration to the extent of their capacity. I also told them that, as a member of the commonwealth, Canada felt that that instrument had in its very concept the opportunity of providing not only for the good of its constituents but for the welfare of all nations in the world, in Asia as well as elsewhere, who are prepared to understand its good intentions and purposes. I also sought to indicate that while there had been differences between Canada and others in the United Nations on recent actions on the part of one member of the commonwealth, because of that difference, while it reflected the objective character of Canada's approach to international affairs as certainly the government saw it, there could be no justification for any nation believing that Canada did not have absolute faith in the character of and the purposes which, generally speaking, Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom seeks to establish. I also sought to indicate that, because we were the closest neighbour of the United States with whom we did not always have full accord in matters having to do with problems affecting our two countries, we had, side by side, over 140 years, lived in peace; and that whatever may be the misgivings of certain countries about that nation it was my judgment, as one Canadian representing my government in Asia, that the basic foreign policy of the United States could only be interpreted as one directed toward the easing of international tension and the preservation of peace in the world.
I will not say that these interpretations were always acceptable but I thought that was the place to say these things, and I said them, I hope, in proper terms and in proper context; and I believe they were accepted as coming from a nation that has gradually built up for itself a reputation for an objective approach in international affairs.
Of course, in Australia and in New Zealand one felt that one was within, as it were, the family circle even though in respect to some matters of recent origin there have been honest differences of view. The position of Australia in this particular is well known. I had the opportunity of discussing these matters with Mr. Menzies, the Prime Minister of Australia, and his foreign minister and, indeed, on one memorable afternoon with all the members of his government. Mr. Menzies said of Canada that notwithstanding what may in particular instances be differences in point of view, one thing that the world

could know of Canada was that it spoke as a member of the commonwealth in the light of what it understood to be its obligations based on no consideration but the good of the commonwealth and the good of all nations throughout the world.
In Ceylon, in India and in Pakistan, notwithstanding the fact that recent events have, understandably, caused a strain on certain relations I found that the situation there now *-based upon my conversations with the three leaders, namely the Prime Minister of Ceylon, Mr. Bandaranaike, Mr. Nehru in India and Prime Minister Suhrawardy in Pakistan-is that there is on their part a recognition of the value of the commonwealth not only as a sensible grouping of nations in this interdependent world but as an instrument which can and is being used to interpret western opinion in many sectors of Asia. I believe that is an important fact to state and to remember. There may be dissident voices in some of these countries but my judgment would be that, for the most part, those who at the present time have to do with the conduct of government in those great countries recognize that in the consultations of prime ministers, in the consultations of commonwealth foreign ministers and in the collaboration that takes place in the United Nations, the commonwealth serves as a valuable instrument in a world that needs to move closer and closer together rather than diverge on an increasing scale.
I took occasion not only to discuss matters in accordance with the mandate given by my colleagues with those responsible for the conduct of government but to visit the people as well. I took occasion to go into their villages. Anyone who knows anything about the complex character of that great Asian state of India will understand what the village means to that country with its 360 millions of people, 80 per cent of whom live in the villages of which there are some half million which have the form, the character and the quality of centuries-old construction. I sought by going amongst the people to indicate, by manner and conduct, that it was the desire of the people of Canada that we should be friends with them, and as well with other nations in Asia, as indeed is the case with other countries in the world who are willing to accept our friendship.
There are some on this continent, and I suspect the same is true in other parts of the world, who possibly misunderstand on occasion a country like India; who sometimes feel that possibly India is disposed, because of its policy of neutralism, to give greater support to those who do not agree with the basic concepts of the free nations

of the world. I should like to say this at once. There is a great undercurrent of spiritual conviction in India, as there is in the case of most of the countries I visited. The religion of Buddha, the Hindu religion, the Moslem religion, the Christian religion, together with the natural instinct so many Asians have for a philosophical bent, in my opinion all these things make these countries an impregnable fortress against the possible encroachment of totalitarian ideals or programs.
Based on these facts and the talks I had in India with many members of the government, with one of them on five occasions and with another on four, I cannot believe that we are justified in suggesting that India would ever embrace dialectal materialism as it is projected to us frequently from the Kremlin or from any other source. This is an important consideration in the kind of world in which we live, where some time there may have to be a decision as to which form of society will prevail ultimately. I am satisfied that while there may not always be political affinity there will be what is even more important, a sort of spiritual affinity between these nations of Asia and the basic concepts of western civilization.
In addition there is another reason for the conclusions I reached. India, Ceylon and Pakistan are deeply dedicated to the democratic form of government and to the parliamentary process. There is no disposition there to accept as efficient or as possible a totalitarian form of government, suppressing, as ultimately that form does, the kind of freedom out of which political maturity can only grow. Of course, that exists in Australia and New Zealand, as it does here. I spend little time on this because it is taken for granted, although in some places on this continent it is not taken for granted that the kind of fundamentals which I have postulated are accepted generally in Asia. I can only say that my belief, and it is a strongly entrenched belief now, is that these principles are widely accepted in India, in Pakistan and in Ceylon.
The Colombo plan came into being in 1951 in Ceylon, in the capital of the country which was the first nation of the commonwealth in that part of Asia which I visited. I think I can say, whether or not we all agree on the extent of the contributions made, that having in mind that the old world extracted from the great Asian land mass much of the wealth of that continent in another day oftentimes for its own benefit, nothing is more salutary in our time, I believe, than the fact that now the western nations of the British commonwealth, in association will) nations in Asia,
The Address-Mr. Martin have joined together for the purpose of promoting the improvement of the economic and social life of the people of Asia. It is a hopeful sign for the improvement of international relations between certain nations of the west and that section of the world that it should be possible for nations like Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain and the United States to share some of their skills and some of their resources according to their capacity with nations whose material standards of life admittedly are not as high as their own. I am firmly of the view that to the extent we follow this course we will be making an important contribution to the peace of the world.
I realize that one must be practical and realistic about the extent to which any nation can go. But, Mr. Speaker, I could not refrain from saying these things to this house, when I think of the hospitals I have visited, the maternity centres I have visited, the eye centres I have seen, the need for medical schools and hospitals and the like. I cannot help but feel that we, through the Colombo plan, are really making a useful contribution in the kind of assistance which we are able to give. I saw a doctor in Chittagong, in east Pakistan, only 10 days ago who had received his degree as an ophthalmologist at the University of Montreal under the Colombo plan. He was the only eye specialist in that part of the country. I saw before him some 300 cases of glaucoma that might have gone without treatment if it had not been for the fact that he had received training under the Colombo plan and in this particular case through Canada.
But one should not for a moment conclude that it is possible through a plan of this sort to take care entirely of the problem of reconstruction in a continent like Asia. The assistance given by the United States, and it is considerable, and by the other participating countries in the Colombo plan, and that assistance too is considerable, is marginal only. If there is going to be a satisfactory measure of reconstruction on the economic and social side in Asia, it will be largely due to the efforts that are now being put forward by the people of Asia themselves. This I clearly indicated to them when I said, on behalf of Canada generally, that our assistance as a Colombo plan power was made without any strings attached. It was not made for the purpose of effecting political alliances or of having them move from positions of neutrality to positions of protagonistic support. I said, what is the case, that our assistance-[DOT] and I indicated we were not all agreed in Canada on what the measure of assistance
188	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Martin
should be-was based upon a sincere appreciation that in this interdependent world our humanitarian obligations demanded of us to render some assistance to those nations and to these people.
While that is the case, I could not help but feel, particularly at the Colombo plan meetings, as I now visualize the political personalities who sat around the conference table, ministers representing every government of the Colombo plan group, that while we might have our differences in economic and social terms, every minister there represented governments that share with us common beliefs in the value of individual freedom, and share with us our view of the importance of the individual human being in his or her relationship to the state, and the belief that, inadequate as it sometimes may be, there is no more effective guarantee for the preservation of human freedom than governments composed of men and women chosen by the people to govern the nation; in other words, a common belief in the parliamentary form of government. And with those common denominators, together with the spiritual foundations, which I have already mentioned, I have no doubt, whether or not we belong to the same military alliances, or the same political grouping, that the vast majority of the nations of Asia with whom I had these contacts can be counted on in the long term to give their expression in support of a society based upon freedom and not on its suppression.
While there was concern in some places about actions taken in Egypt, there were strong denunciations about the aggression of the Soviet union in Hungary. I spoke on one occasion to the Indian council on world affairs. I do not know whether there were reports here of this meeting, but some critical comment was made by one or two individuals who interpolated questions at the meeting. I said in my remarks that there was a vast difference between the attitude of Great Britain and of France toward their obligations under the charter of the United Nations and the reaction of the Soviet union not to one but to 10 resolutions passed in the assembly against the aggression it perpetrated in Hungary. The difference in the two cases was that in the one there was an acceptance on the part of the charged parties, if you like, of the resolution taken by the United Nations and in the other a complete flouting of the resolutions passed by the United Nations. And that I regard as a matter of the greatest significance.
It would be wrong for me to overlook in this account the important work of the international supervisory commissions in

Indo-China. Whenever I use the phrase "Indochina" now I remember the correction made by a distinguished Australian who told me that I should no longer speak of Indo-China but rather of three countries in Indo-China. Indo-China is no longer a fact although at one time it did represent a geographical entity. Now there is no Indo-China but North and South Viet Nam, a nation in its undivided quality representing 20 millions of people; Cambodia, representing 3 million people; and Laos, a small nation representing li million people. In each of these there is now a rivalry of varying dimensions for supremacy between competing interests.
The house will recall that the international supervisory commissions came into being not as a result of the action of the United Nations but of the accord arrived at in Geneva in 1954 by the great powers. Canada is represented on the three international supervisory commissions that exist in these countries. The chairman is a national of India and the third member is from Poland. If one wanted an example of the effectiveness of a United Nations paramilitary force in action to meet a specific ad hoc purpose one finds it in the three international supervisory commissions. Those three commissions have kept the peace in an area of the world that threatened us all, the house will recall, some two and one-half years ago. When those commissions will be able to finish their work I cannot say. Many Canadians are serving on these three commissions. I would like to pay a tribute, on the occasion of my return to the house, to the work of our fellow citizens who during the past two years, under the most trying of circumstances, have upheld the dignity and the honour of this nation.
It is difficult, I know, to translate one's feelings about a matter such as this, and I am not doing it to the extent that I possibly could if I were less fatigued and better prepared; but I would like the house to appreciate for one moment the significance of an international supervisory body that has its scene of operations away up in the mountains of Laos, in a primitive part of the country, where the march of civilization seemingly has made but little impress, and where the troops of the royal government occupy strategic hills in their several thousands, and not far away are the forces of the Pathet Lao group, forces that have received assistance from the so-called Chinese People's Republic and from the Soviet union, both holding fixed positions, positions that

represent the situation on the date of ceasefire but who, thanks to the stabilizing influence of the international supervisory commission, are not at war but at peace with one another.
We shall hear more of these three countries in the course of the ensuing period. They may not be the most powerful countries in the world but they do occupy geographic areas of strategic interest, not only geographically but in terms of the acceptance or the rejection of political forces that are basic, Mr. Speaker, in the troubled world which confronts all of us. No one man represents Asia. When he was in Washington Mr. Nehru is reported to have said that he did not seek to be the single spokesman for Asia. I can well understand now what he meant and why he made that statement; but he hoped to provide a bridge between one important section of the western world and Asia. I believe that Mr. Nehru is the bridge between that section of the world and those sections of the west who respect his judgment and who understand the basic purposes of his policies. It would be easy and popular to join in decrying some of his actions but I shall not do that because I believe more strongly than ever before that in the interests of world peace if we are going to have a proper acceptance on the part of Asia of our good intentions we for our part must recognize the dominating motives of the present great prime minister of India.
For us he has great respect and in our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the President of the United States he has great confidence, as he has in other political leaders in other parts of the world, and the existence of this confidence is a most important matter.
I saw Mr. Nehru for a few moments immediately upon his return from the United States and Canada; I saw him the next morning and later again that day. I found in him the same disposition to understand other points of view in a spirit of tolerance that I personally had experienced at the United Nations in my relations with spokesmen of India. It is not always possible to agree but it is essential, if constructive efforts are to be made, that there should exist a capacity to appreciate the reasons for certain attitudes and approaches. It is in this way that differences are composed and agreements are achieved.
I do not believe one can attach too great importance to the acceptance by political leaders of the good intentions of others and their appreciation of the factors involved in differing attitudes. Given conditions of this
The Address-Mr. Martin kind and an absence of vituperation in the conduct of one nation with another, I think it is possible to work out solutions that will result in a satisfactory disposition of the problems that divide mankind at this time.
I was not the only one travelling in Asia at this time. There were more important political personalities than myself, holding higher offices and representing greater power numerically and perhaps influentially. I could not hope to emulate some of the receptions accorded them or the influence which for the time being they may have sought to exercise. I spoke in one village to about 10,000 people one day where others only a week before spoke to several hundreds of thousands. We did not speak of the same things and I am sure that behind the things that were said there were different motivations and intentions.
I spoke of international friendship, of the importance of social and economic reconstruction and of improvements in health and living standards, of our belief in the value of the United Nations as an instrument for the discussion, and we trust ultimately the resolving, of some major world problems that divide us at this time. Behind my simple observations was based the pattern that comes from a belief in spiritual values, that comes from a belief in individual freedom as opposed to totalitarian power through which millions of people are caused to accept the dictates of a small group which constitutes itself as the government of the day. No one can tell whether my peregrinations will have the kind of effect which I in moments of deep sincerity would like to think possible. But I would say this, that as one man in the face of the situation attending that tremendously interesting and complicated continent, I did my best to put forward not only the point of view of the government of Canada and of all shades of political opinion but as well the point of view of all the people of Canada. In my discussions with members of governments, of course, I could only speak for the government of Canada. I would like to think I did put forward in those private talks, the results of which I hope will in the not too distant future become apparent, the point of view which we on this side believe to be the most desirable position to take.
I come back from this experience, Mr. Speaker, not as an expert but more humble than ever in the face of the great problems that stagger mankind in Asia today as they do elsewhere. I return confident in the belief that if we observe the principles embodied in the charter of the United Nations, if we employ the media of adjudication and conciliation instead of force, if we bear in mind at the same time that every country has its

The Address-Mr. W. M. Johnson own problems and its own way of dealing with them, then assuming the necessary conditions of good faith, we shall, as mankind has in the past, surmount the tremendous issues that confront us all.
Having said all these things I would not want to indicate to the people of Asia, whose guest I was, who extended me their friendship and their collaboration, whose members of government listened understanding^ to what I had to say on behalf of my colleagues, that I now make invidious comparisons between my country and the lot of the people of Asia. That is not my purpose when I say that having had the experience of visiting lands where long before this country came into being there was deep theological and philosophic thought, having in mind the fact that the industrial revolution has not touched them as it has reached us and as a consequence has not given them the same material benefits it has given us, I will not be misunderstood when I say to this house that I return to my seat, I come back to Canada convinced more than ever before of the richness of our heritage.
I can only express the hope that all of us will in the face of our good fortune seek to give expression to Him who in the final analysis is responsible for many advantages that have not yet been opened to peoples in other areas, and that this will stir us on to recognize that we are all our brothers' keepers in this interdependent world. Unless this attitude and the policy of the good neighbour prevails, we cannot look forward to the fulfilment of what we want to see realized in our times and for our children, those things without which we cannot preserve responsible measures of security and freedom in a world at peace.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like at the outset to express the hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will reserve some of his energies in order to make a 50-minute address in this chamber to convince his colleagues of the desirability of introducing a comprehensive national health insurance plan.
I welcome the opportunity of participating again in this debate on the speech from the throne, and it will not be surprising to many members to learn that the subject of my speech is the problems which it is my duty and responsibility to present before this house. The problems that confront those in my constituency are not too different from those confronting all agricultural constituencies in western Canada and, in some measure, throughout all Canada. There is, it will be appreciated, a limitation of time on this debate, and 1 will therefore not be able to deal


with all the problems which are confronting agriculture in Canada. I shall therefore limit my remarks specifically to matters affecting western Canada and those whom I represent in the Kindersley constituency.
Members representing other areas of Canada, if they have farmers within their constituencies, will have an appreciation of the problems confronting all these people and will, I feel, give consideration to what I have to say so they may better appreciate the peculiar circumstances which have existed in western Canada for the past five years. These are growing problems which, to my mind, are much greater than those which affect any other parts of Canada because after all, Mr. Speaker, agriculture is the backbone of our economy and western Canada has for decades played an important part in that economy.
I think we could say that the treatment which the present Liberal government has given agriculture over the past number of years is very shabby indeed. I am not going to condemn everything the Liberal government has done; it is not to be expected that in the 21 years during which they have been in power they could have blundered all the time. Some of the legislation they have introduced must have reflected the desires of the farmers in Canada. The comments and criticisms I am going to make in connection with agricultural problems are constructively intended to present our views to the government for their consideration and action and, as is characteristic of members of the C.C.F. party, I am not going to confine myself to criticism but am going to suggest solutions and policies that this government should adopt immediately.
It has been conceded generally that farmers all across Canada are being caught in the ever-tightening vise of cost-price squeeze. The cost of everything that we as farmers have to buy is going up and up while the price we receive for our products is continually declining. Today a western farmer is required to pay $7,000 for a self-propelled combine needed to harvest his crop. Seven thousand dollars is the price of a pretty good quarter-section of land in many areas, and members will appreciate what that means, when one piece of farm machinery equals the price of a quarter-section of land. The cost of repairs and fuel has also increased and, in addition, farmers are confronted with the problem of getting adequate labour to help in the operation of their farms. They have found that because of the continuously hazardous nature of agricultural production it is impossible to guarantee year-round employment to hired help. As a result they have to pay very high wages indeed in order

to induce men to work on the farm. They have to ask for high wages because they, too, require security. This problem is becoming a very serious one indeed, Mr. Speaker, and it is felt in many areas that measures will have to be taken to assist farmers in securing full-time or part-time hired help. To this end I have introduced the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act so as to provide coverage for agricultural workers.
It is my opinion that this will provide one solution, and I hope that when the matter is debated in the House of Commons favourable consideration will be given to that subject.
Along with these increasing costs which I have mentioned is the item of freight rates, which are increasing by leaps and bounds every year. Let us look on the price side. Members will find that the prices farmers are receiving are declining year by year. In 1950 farmers received $1.85 a bushel for their wheat. Today it is $1.40, both prices being at the head of the lakes with the farmers paying the freight on their wheat. The price of beef, eggs and poultry has declined this year. Last fall you could buy a calf at the Edmonton stockyards for $25. The Economic Annalist in the October issue, using the years 1935/39 as equalling 100 as a basis, points out that the cost of commodities and services to the farmer this year stood at a record high of 254.3, an increase of 24.3 points in the last five years. The price received for field crops stood at 171.1, a decrease of 29.3 in the last five years. In other words, in 1951 the cost price was separated by 29.6 points and in 1956 it was separated by the colossal amount of 83.2 points.
The cost of production of bountiful crops has naturally increased, and this has been reflected in the economic position of the farmers. In the Kindersley vocational farm management survey it is pointed out that out of 83 farms, only 65 per cent of all farms in this sample were able to realize the total cost of production on the basis of a yield of 24 bushels an acre, and not on the basis of the amount of wheat they were able to sell. This report goes on to indicate that the average cost of production for the 83 farms stands at $17.49 per crop acre basis, allowing no wage for the operator; with an operator's wage it stands at $24.61 per acre. It is apparent that the farmers in western Canada are indeed suffering because of the glut of wheat which has developed in Canada.
Judging from many of the reports we see in the newspapers and announcements by government leaders we are tempted to rush
The Address-Mr. W. M. Johnson out to the granary to see if we have any wheat left, because those reports indicate it is being sold so rapidly that we are not going to have any left with which to fill our quota. But when you do go out to the granary you find the bottom six inches or one foot rotted, because after all the wheat has been there since 1952 or 1953.
The true picture is presented in the November issue of the Wheat Review, and I quote:
Total supplies of Canadian wheat for 1956-57 are estimated at 1,075 million bushels, consisting of the July 31, 1956 carryover of 537 million and the new crop of 538 million. A supply of the size indicated is the largest on record, 8 per cent above that of last year and exceeding the previous record of 998 million set in 1953-54.
That is the true picture. It is interesting to note that of the four major exporting countries, Canada is the only one with an increase in supply. There has been some indication that the delivery position is improving. At this time last year we had delivered only 83.6 million bushels during the period August 1 to December 19, while this year we have delivered 122.5 million bushels. Those deliveries must be compared with the ten-year average of 201.2 million bushels. It is quite apparent that our stocks are increasing because our sales are not increasing in proportion to the amount being grown.
It is apparent that the long-term solution of this problem must be along the lines of a more aggressive sales policy. Some might scoff at that and ask where we are going to sell more wheat, but I have here an indication where we can do so. I have here an extract from a paper prepared by the foreign agricultural service for the wheat commodity section of the 34th annual national agricultural outlook conference held in Washington, which indicates that the possibilities for the export of wheat will be much more favourable during the coming year. It states:
Exports July-October 1956-57 amounted to 160.4 million bushels, virtually twice as great as the 81.5 million bushels shipped in the same period a year earlier.
Exports for dollars are expected to be greater, especially to the northern European countries where poor harvesting weather together with the severe damage suffered in early 1956 have materially decreased domestic crops. Also, this situation will curtail wheat exports from France and some of those markets will be supplied by the United States.
There is an indication of an ever-expanding world market, and Canada must take its share of that market. As it presently stands, the impact of this increasing world market has been in the form of even lower quotas on the average to western Canada. When the government changed their policy last year and decided that no effort would be made to equalize the quotas, complete

The Address-Mr. W. M. Johnson chaos reigned. We found some points that ended the crop year with a 4-bushel quota; some with 5 and some with 7. That certainly seemed inherently unfair and was protested by the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the Saskatchewan farmers' union. It was protested in the House of Commons by members of the C.C.F. group, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce assured us that those points which had a low quota would be given priority at the start of the new crop year to equalize their opportunity. That promise has never been filled.
We find that as of January 4 there are still three marketing points in western Canada on a unit quota; 478 are on a 1-bushel quota; 962 are on 2-bushels, 469 on 3-bushels and 140 on 4. Over two-thirds of the marketing points are on a 2-bushel quota or less, and I suspect that many of those points that are on quotas up to 4 bushels have not had an opportunity to deliver their grain.
There should be a much greater attempt to equalize these quotas in order to give each farmer an opportunity to share in the return from the sale of his grain. While consideration is being given to this problem, consideration should also be given to the problem of the allocation of box cars to marketing points on a more equitable basis. There is something else which has been requested consistently by farm organizations, and that is the allocation of box cars to the elevator of the farmer's choice.
The government does not seem to be concerned with these vexing problems, and there has been no spurt of activity to deal with them. Indeed the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) has indicated that he is not even going to bother appointing a transport controller. On January 9 I asked the Minister of Transport, as reported on page 24 of Hansard, the following:
In view of the termination of the duties of the former transport controller at the conclusion of navigation last December 17, can the minister make an announcement that an appointment has been made to fill this important post.
The minister replied;
Regardless of the impression of the hon. member, the resignations of the transport controller and of the deputy transport controller were received only in the last week of December.
Later on I asked this question:
Am I to assume that there will be an appointment made at a very early date.
To this the minister replied as follows:
I think I should say this, that the transport controller carried out his duties with outstanding success in the face of very substantial criticism from the hon. gentleman opposite. In the first place, I think it is going to be exceedingly difficult for the government to find a transport controller of the caliber of Mr. Milner. In the second place.
[Mr. Johnson (Kindersley) .1
I think in view of the criticism expressed by my hon. friend it will be very difficult for us to find someone who will be willing to accept the duties.
I would be the last one to deny that I have attempted to reflect the views of western farm organizations in a critical manner in relation to the way in which the transport controller has carried out his duties. It is significant that in the recommendations of the interprovincial farm union council is included a recommendation that a full-time transport controller be appointed with sufficient power to exercise the responsibility of making available sufficient numbers of box cars for the movement of grain. The Saskatchewan wheat pool has been on record consistently as objecting to the manner in which the former controller dealt with this problem. At one time the Minister of Transport indicated that he was not going to allow this position to remain vacant. Discussing the Department of Transport Act on April 25, 1956, as reported on page 3271 of Hansard, the minister said:
I do not believe that an operation so complex as the movement of grain from the western provinces to the Pacific coast or to the lakehead and thence to Atlantic ports is something that can be left without direction.
Yet we have the situation that this same minister has left this important post unfilled for nearly one full month. During that month we had a tie-up of the Canadian Pacific Railway which further complicated the movement of grain in bulk. The minister might say that he received the resignation from Mr. Milner only at a very recent date, but I would point out that, as found at page 314 of the proceedings of the committee on agriculture of July 6, 1956, Mr. Milner states this:
As I shall not be transport controller after the close of navigation this year, this occasion gives me the only opportunity . . .
And so on. It is just another indication, Mr. Speaker, of the irresponsibility of the present Liberal government in dealing with these grave domestic crises.
The government's solution to this problem has been to institute this despised system of bank loans, namely a system requiring the farmers to pay 5 per cent interest on what is in effect their own wages. The impracticability of that system has certainly been proven by the number of farmers who have been able to take advantage of the scheme. The farm organizations have requested the immediate adoption of a cash advance proposal on a permanent basis. This would give an opportunity to equalize the returns of farmers on unequal quotas. A farmer on a unit quota would then have the opportunity, which is justifiably his, of getting some return on his grain rather than being obliged to

wait several months until the quota has been increased. The Gordon commission indicates that it is necessary to adopt this principle in part.
That would seem to be one point on which I could find myself in agreement with the Gordon commission. Yes, we must have a permanent system of cash advances in order to allow the farmers to have the income with which to meet their debts.
I would call on the government right now to make an immediate interim payment on last year's pool. This would be more valuable than any other single factor which the government could deal with at the present time. I estimate that there would be funds available for an interim payment of between 10 and 12 cents to be made in the very near future. I would warn the government that the financial position of the farmer is such that he is not in a position to wait for them to hand it out as a pre-election bribe in the form of a fatter annual final payment. The farmers who find they have huge piles of wheat out on the ground are not going to be fooled in that way.
I point out that the final solution to this problem, of course, is an increased trade policy to deal with the ever-expanding markets of the future. In the meantime the government should certainly give the farmers some assistance and some guidance in the selection of crops. I have seen many farmers who were in a complete quandary, not knowing what to grow for the future. Some farmers in my constituency tried growing Argentine rape, only to have it frozen. Others have tried flax on land unsuited for flax. Others have tried and are trying field peas in an attempt to diversify, in order to dodge the blows which the federal government seems determined to level at agriculture. Instead of using the agricultural conference which is held each fall as a means of giving a guide to our farmers, they just have it as a casual little meeting where a great many pious statements are made, but when you boil them all down there is no guide for the farmer. The farmer is not told to grow more Durum, more flax, more wheat or more barley. He is left entirely to his own devices.
I have pointed out many of the factors with regard to which this government has fallen down in dealing with agricultural problems in Canada, but the biggest problem of all is the complete absence of an agricultural policy. Oh, you might say that we have an Agricultural Prices Support Act, which in reality is nothing but a patchwork of support prices and guarantees, each below the market 82715-13
The Address-Mr. Bruneau price. There is no program for agricultural credit. There is no program to guarantee* the farmers a fair return for their produce. I should like to see this government adopt a comprehensive agricultural policy which would incorporate these features and give agriculture all across Canada a fair share of the national income, that is to say, give to the farmers of Canada a parity with other occupations.
I think it is only right that we should have that policy, because the farmers are certainly one class who are deserving of it. I should like to see this agricultural policy include price supports and price levels which would guarantee a reasonable standard of living to the family farm. It is a workable proposal which may, as the Saskatchewan wheat pool indicates, involve deficiency payments to producers. I think the adoption of an agricultural policy would do more than any other thing to resolve the dilemma which confronts us at the present time. The Edmonton Journal in a news story on Friday, November 16, 1956, had this to say under the heading "Liberals Say Farmers Unhappy at Policies":
The closing sessions of the Alberta Liberal association's annual convention Wednesday, said farmers were uphappy with farm policies.
Rulon Dahl of Raymond, Alta., said the average farmer in the west is not satisfied. "If we are to win the next election, we must smarten up the farm picture".
I think you will find many farmers in Canada who will agree with that speaker, and who feel that the Liberals must certainly smarten up the farm picture. But on the basis of their past record there is really no hope. It will take the C.C.F., through their role as an effective opposition or as the government, to provide fair treatment for what is still the basic industry of Canada, namely agriculture.
