speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me at this moment to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare on his extremely interesting description of his good-will mission around the world.
When the members of this house assembled on January 8 in the Senate chamber to hear the message from His Excellency, the representative of the Queen, I am sure we all had the feeling that the present session would be of the greatest importance. I for one have been much more impressed with this idea after hearing the speech from the throne, which reflects the powerful impetus our country is experiencing under the enlightened guidance of the present government. May Providence continue to inspire those who

The Address-Mr. Bruneau
share in the heavy task of governing the country, and shower countless gifts upon our population.
Even if this does not mean that all is for the best in the best of worlds we may, however, consider ourselves a most privileged nation, which is now well on the way to becoming one of the most essential wheels in the gearbox of world affairs. Both on the international and the national levels Canada has shown in recent events its capacity to stand at the outposts of foreign affairs for the preservation of peace and the advancement of the human race. Only a few weeks ago our government, through our most able and distinguished Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson )and other members of the Canadian delegation to the United Nations, was the keystone in solving many of the Middle Eastern problems including the Suez canal crisis.
Moreover, a point has been reached now where no major decision on western policies can be taken without Canada being consulted. Our influence in international affairs is constantly growing, both because of the policy of our government on external affairs and the sound and comprehensive interpretation of our national problems. The well-established policies of the government on international affairs are agreed upon and supported by all including, I am sure, hon. members of the opposition. I shall, then, refrain from taking any more of the time of the house on this matter. I would feel guilty, however, if I did not mention our hope to see our country continue to be the guiding light and an effective worker in the task of healing many of the sore spots still threatening world peace.
May I at this point also congratulate the government for the efficiency and spontaneity with which they offered help to the Hungarian people who were forced by the communist persecutors to flee from their homeland. These martyrs to the cause of human freedom are most welcome to Canada because our nation wants to be in the forefront of those nations giving aid to these people who did not hesitate to sacrifice everything for the right to live as free citizens. They will be a great asset to our country in the future. Evidently new blood is needed to maintain the steady progress Canada has experienced during the last few years. With the enlightening advice contained in some of the conclusions drawn by the royal commission on economic prospects, there is no doubt but that the government will be in a position to use this increased manpower to the best economic advantage for the good of

the country. It has shown already that it can give a stable and vigorous economy.
Incidentally, may I say that so stable and vigorous is the Canadian economy at present that it has hardly been disturbed by the recent railway strike, for the settlement of which the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet deserve to be highly commended. Some disturbances have occurred, as was to be expected, but they were of minor importance compared to what would have happened in a country with a staggering economy. However, that industrial dispute was a very serious one and had many ill effects on many sectors of the country. I noticed, for instance, that many remote areas were suddenly cut away from the economic life of the country, and this affected the daily life of the people as well as their daily productivity, small though it may have been. I see in this fact additional proof of the need for the decentralization of our manufacturing industries, both primary and secondary.
In the speech from the throne the government has indicated its intention to recommend the establishment of a committee to consider what should be done to make better use of the land for agriculture, and thus to contribute more effectively to the improvement of agricultural production and the incomes of those engaged in it.
(Translation):
In seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne, my hon. friend the member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) mentioned all the benefits that our farming class and our people in general can expect from that measure which, he said, is very promising indeed for the future. I agree with him completely and I take this opportunity to congratulate him on the excellent speech he made in this house in seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
(Text):
By the same token, may I also extend my hearty congratulations to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) on the very keen and interesting views he put forward in proposing the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
The principles underlying the setting up of the proposed committee to study the means of making better use of land for agriculture are of the same vintage as those calling for a similar measure to study the possibilities of drawing a master plan to decentralize industry in this country. It will be recalled that last year during the budget debate I made such a suggestion. Those who have had the opportunity of perusing the preliminary re-

port of the royal commission on economic prospects, tabled in this house last week, must realize that many findings of the commission call for such decentralization and for the better use of areas outside large centres which are suitable for manufacturing industry. One could be convinced that such a move would benefit agriculture as well as the manufacturing industry.
For instance, paragraph 17, chapter 2, of the Gordon preliminary report states that Canada is becoming an increasingly urban country and that this trend will continue. It is predicted that over the period running from 1951 to 1980 the proportion of the population living in metropolitan and urban areas of more than 100,000 people may represent from 36 to 56 per cent of the entire Canadian population. Is this expectation to become a reality, or should not something be done to alleviate the trend? Everyone knows that overpopulated metropolitan and urban areas are amongst the worst enemies of a sound and growing economy. I demonstrated that point last year, and I shall not take the time of this house to repeat what I said then. I will point out again, however, that in my own constituency of Glengarry-Prescott there are scores of communities suitable for industrial purposes, either for the establishment of new industries or the re-establishment of previously existing industries. The same situation, I am sure, prevails in dozens of other constituencies.
In Glengarry-Prescott we have all the facilities. I know that other areas cannot secure manufacturing industries because of lack of hydro-electric power. With the advent of dieselization and the coming use of atomic energy for industrial purposes I do not think this will constitute a problem any longer. In any case this is one of the points into which the committee or royal commission I suggested last year would have to investigate. Had such a body been formed last year it could have laid down the main foundation of its work after the publication of the report of the Gordon commission. Now that the preliminary report is out, I think it is more than ever the time for the government to give all its attention to such a measure if we are to draw up a policy capable of influencing the economic life of Canada in the course of the next 25 years.
To further help the economy of the manufacturing industries; to ease the housing situation in the big cities; to provide for better and more logical distribution of industrial products, decentralization would give more impetus to the agricultural areas benefiting from it. The increase of population it would bring in those semi-urban regions normally 827I5-13J
The Address-Mr. Bruneau, would increase the local consumption of agricultural products grown nearby, thereby reducing the cost of transportation and consequently lowering the cost of living.
Another effect of decentralization would be to get more agricultural manpower on the farm. The Gordon preliminary report also points out that in agriculture output is expected to decline in round figures from 13 per cent to 6 per cent of the total output. Here again I think efforts should be made to alleviate such a trend. In my humble opinion the boosting of regional economy and the keeping of agricultural manpower on the farms would be two very important steps in the right direction.
Since the preliminary report of the royal commission on economic prospects has been tabled, economics have been paramount in most parliamentary and political circles. It is surely a subject of prime importance, and I think in a democratic and peace-loving country like ours a sound economy is possible only if all classes of society are assured of a decent living and of freedom from want. That is why the government initiated a program of social security some years ago.
Some of my colleagues who have preceded me in this debate have voiced their views on the subject. I should like very briefly to emphasize the importance it has for the people of Canada. When speaking of social security one thinks almost immediately of old age pensions. The number of people for whom this measure means the difference between a very frugal living and dire poverty is unbelievable, and statistics do not always reflect that. What these old people receive now under the Old Age Pensions Act, however, is merely sufficient to subsist on. When it was increased to $40 a month the old age pension came as a benediction from heaven for those who had nothing to live on, and even then it could not buy for them all they needed; but nowadays it is felt that this amount is utterly insufficient.
We all know that the cost of living has skyrocketed during the last few years. It has also skyrocketed for old people, especially for those who have no other source of income but this pension. That is why I would suggest the increase be possibly $25 a month, bringing the pension to $65 a month for all old age pensioners, with a means test for those who are between 65 and 70 years of age. Also, if we are to help the Canadian people to keep pace with the constantly rising cost of living, I feel that family allowances should be increased accordingly, let us say to possibly $5 to $7 on the basic allowance, with an equivalent increase for other classes.

The Address-Mr. Bruneau
In that regard I am also very sorry to deplore the fact that it has been impossible up to now to implement the health insurance plan that the Canadian government proposed last year. It is to be hoped that some of the provinces will not continue to minimize the importance of such a scheme of social security to our country.
In the speech from the throne the government has shown once again its appreciation of the interrelation between the various activities which are to make Canada a great country in the future. It is very gratifying indeed to know that hon. members will be asked to approve the establishment of the Canada Council for arts, humanities and social sciences. Although those three fields are not directly connected with the administration of the country, they must be considered as the inspiration of the leaders and as vital factors in the superiority of a nation.
This new council will be called upon to grant many scholarships and bursaries, especially to young Canadians. I would like, then, to suggest that it could be attached, for administrative purposes, to a new department of youth which I have advocated many times in this house. Under the same new youth department could come the administration of the increased annual grants to universities, to be distributed by the national conference of Canadian universities, for the purpose of helping our institutions of higher learning to prepare the future leaders of our country.
On that measure, which has been so widely approved throughout Canada, I will mention my belief that the national conference of Canadian universities, having undertaken to act as a distributing agent of those grants, should immediately start an inquiry to determine the various needs of each university, aside from construction projects. As it is now, the plan calls for the distribution of the grants on a per capita basis of the student population. These per capita grants undoubtedly will constitute a great factor in the development of our universities, but it is also evident that some universities are not in quite the same position as others, either because of local conditions or because of their growing influence, which calls for a more extensive and faster development.
I am not suggesting that grants should be given on a discriminatory basis, but simply that a study should be made with a view to extending on a rational basis, some additional help to institutions that are capable of absolutely proving their need of money for new equipment or additional personnel, for instance.
The speech from the throne also mentioned that a measure will be placed before the

house for the purpose of renewing, on a revised and increased basis, the federal program of amounts to provincial governments in aid of technical and vocational training. This is another item which could be administered by a new youth department. Everybody knows how useful technical and vocational training has been in Canada since the inception of the Roger plan. Incidentally, is it not a little strange that the skin of certain provincial governments is not so tender when it comes time to accepting federal grants in this particular field of education? Is it that they consider technical and vocational training so much less important than university training, or is it an effort to continue an established tradition, hoping that people of particular provinces will not notice the inconsistency of their attitude? Whatever the reason is, this plan is accepted even by the most discriminatory province and I heartily support it, because it is aimed at bettering the conditions of life of the working classes who are the active nucleus of our free enterprise system.
There are many other points in the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, that are of high interest to all Canadian people. I only wanted to emphasize a few points which I consider of prime importance to the country at large and to my constitutents in particular. Briefly, I think the present session has started out under very good auspices. Canada is near the top with respect to influence in international affairs. The economic outlook of the country is better than ever, both in view of our growing activities and a stable economy, and we can say that there is nothing to fear in the future as long as our administrators will make it their duty to pave the way for our future leaders. Nevertheless, those bright prospects, most of which have been emphasized in the Gordon preliminary report, will not materialize unless we start immediately to implement some measures to make sure that the great majority of Canadian citizens will benefit from those gifts of nature.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the few remarks I wanted to submit very humbly to the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much interested in hearing some of the observations made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, by reason of the fact that he may have an opportunity to vote for the increase in the old age pension and possibly the increase in the family allowance which he has indicated he thinks is necessary. So far as his observations concerning a national health plan are concerned, I would point out that it is most unfortunate that this government has

such little confidence in the scheme itself that it has not proposed to make it possible for those provinces which have indicated they wish to share in it to have at least the opportunity of discovering whether or not the plan will work.
It is so often the case that "the best-laid schemes o' mice an' men gang aft agley". It was my intention to speak of some of the questions that my own people regard as vital in their particular orbit. I am thinking of specific problems in connection with dredging and fishing; old age pensioners' problems; customs and revenue problems, and certain others about which people in my constituency approach me from time to time. However, in today's Globe and Mail I found an article which gives me a great deal of concern. It is probable that it would be viewed with considerable alarm by the people in British Columbia if there were any truth to the matter, and I have every reason to believe that the article is quite accurate. The article appears in the column headed "B.C. Letter" and is found on the financial page of the Globe and Mail of Monday, January 14, 1957. The article is entitled "Forest Industry Woes Affect Whole Economy" and was written from Vancouver by Nigel Dunn. The first paragraph reads:
British Columbia's vital forest industry is in trouble. It is suffering from the effects of an increasingly sticky market; and it can expect to suffer more from the demands of labour.
A good many people of course are all too frequently inclined to blame labour for most of our ills, but history has proven that in my province labour and management have made a habit of resolving their difficulties to the mutual satisfaction of both, and I am sure this will be the case in this instance as well. However, further down in the report we find this notation:
British Columbia's forest industry is a $500 million a year operation. It employs more than 50,000 men. ... In addition to the many big companies whose capitalization is counted in tens of millions of dollars, there are more than 1,000 small logging companies whose existence depends completely on the prosperity of the major producers for which they work.
If by reason of the fact that we have lost our export markets, or if the forestry industry in British Columbia is curtailed in any other way, it will be more serious, as far as the people of my province are concerned, than the rail strike which we have just experienced. I venture to say it would not only be much more serious but would be viewed with considerably more alarm. The article goes on to say:
British Columbia is losing its lumber markets abroad as a result of the prosperity which it has
The Address-Mr. Hahn helped to create. Its important British market is shrinking alarmingly because of skyrocketing ocean freight rates.
We find the responsibility rests completely with this government in the establishment of freight rates to and from ports of entry in British Columbia. This is a difficulty which only this government can resolve, and if our market is shrinking as this article indicates then I would say this government has the responsibility to look into this question immediately in order to see if something can be done concerning the high freight rates we are subjected to in ocean navigation. The article continues:
Its United States market-the biggest single buyer of British Columbia forest products-has been cut back because of United States credit restrictions on home construction.
I am fully aware that it is impossible for us as Canadians to determine what should be the credit restrictions in the United States. However, I am also aware that this government was advised a year or more ago by many 'hon. members in this house that we were becoming altogether too dependent on United States markets, and that this dependency would some day put us in a difficult economic condition if we should lose those markets. Apparently we are reaching that point today. The fact is that our government has put all its eggs into one basket in the export field.
As recently as last week the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) indicated to the chamber of commerce in Portland, Oregon, that the people of the United States would be expected to buy more goods from Canada so we could have a better balance of trade. The very fact that this government through its economic policy has made it impossible and impractical to keep the market we did have with Great Britain and other European countries has had the effect of denying to us as British Columbians and as Canadians the business we normally should have which would keep in operation our great forest industry.
The article says further:
Ocean freight rates are only part of the reason for the decline in the usual $60 million worth of lumber imported by Britain from British Columbia.
. . . The 25 per cent decline in house building estimated to result in the United States this year is expected to decrease even more British Columbia's exports south of the border in 1957.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I can only re-emphasize what I drew to your attention earlier, and I trust through you to the government, that it is necessary for us to find markets other than in the United States to

speechtext:
The opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of speaking to this House of Commons on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is appreciated by all of us in western Canada. It is an opportunity for me to present the views of the great constituency of Swift Current-Maple Creek, and also to make a few observations on the state of the nation, as it is called to the south of us. Congratulations would, of necessity, be in order to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the splendid address. The contributions they made were appreciated by all members of this house, and that appreciation has been voiced by them.
So far as we Liberals are concerned, that is what we expect of other Liberals. We expect not the common but the uncommon; we expect nothing mediocre; we expect the

The Address-Mr. Studer extraordinary, not the ordinary, and that is what the Liberals who sit in this house endeavour to present. I would, therefore, like to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. They are a source of pride to each and every one of us.
By their deeds we shall know them. Since it was my privilege to speak in this house last year I think everyone will agree that progress has been made in Canada. Not all the difficulties have been solved, but I think no one will disagree with the statement that progress has been made. This is a better country in which to live than it was last year. If that is true, and I think you will all agree that it is, then we must have had a government and government policies that made that possible. With the help of all, including the opposition, I am sure that next year, when at least the government and all its members will be back again, perhaps in greater numbers, the people of Canada will again agree that progress has been made in this country. How can Liberal policies have a different effect? What else could you expect from policies that, through experience, have been proven to be adaptable to the needs of the Canadian people and which will bring Canada to the heights that every Canadian expects?
My constituency of Swift Current-Maple Creek is, as you all know, predominantly agricultural. In every session I have endeavoured to present to you some of the good things that come from that constituency. However, agriculture is not the only means by which the people of the constituency make a living. We have a great number of labouring people who make a great contribution to the welfare of Canada. We have railway people, and there are two divisional points in the constituency, Swift Current itself and Shaunavon. The people in that area are almost entirely dependent upon the Canadian Pacific Railway, so you would expect them to be happy that a solution was found to the rail strike which was so detrimental not only to that area of western Canada but to all areas in Canada dependent upon that great service organization. Irrespective of the motives for that strike it has been settled, and I was pleased that all members of the opposition congratulated the government on the form of the settlement and the fact that it was settled without compulsion. May it ever be that all strikes in this country when they originate-perhaps one could call them the penalties of democracy but I would rather call them one of the rights of democracy, that any individual organization in the country has the right to strike because any time that right does not exist then in my opinion


we no longer have a democracy-will be settled without compulsion. We in western Canada are grateful to the government for promoting a settlement of the strike.
I am more familiar, Mr. Speaker, with agriculture than with any other activity, because I have lived with it practically all my life. I consider it, as perhaps all of you consider the occupation in which you are engaged, as one of the most important contributions to the welfare of the country. I would submit that in the great economic expansion of Canada the most important industry in Canada was agriculture. Let us never accept the idea that we can depend on all the other industries for our advancement and leave agriculture on its own. It seems to be inherent in human nature that we take agriculture for granted. As a result it is necessary for agriculture, throughout the years, to make appeals to governments for assistance.
We often wonder why that is so. Why is it necessary for agriculture to apply for assistance to the Canadian government or other governments in the world? It should be the other way around; every other industry in Canada should be making the appeals that agriculture is making, because agriculture should be in the preferred position. Agriculture should never have to appeal, shall we say, or go in a begging manner to the government of Canada or the government of any other country.
I am trying to tell this parliament that the people of this country cannot exist without agriculture. All flesh is grass, and from grass everything in the form of flesh is originated. If you took grass out of existence, if it refused to grow for even one year, there would be no life in existence any longer. The importance of agriculture is not at any time overemphasized. It is more important than any other vocation, and I do not wish to deprecate any other vocation. It is more important than any other business, and the same holds true in regard to any other endeavour or any other profession or any corporation or any government. Without agriculture there could be no existence.
Have you noted this, that wherever new settlement takes place, whether it is in a new country or within an area, the first thought is not whether we shall have business, not whether there shall be lawyers-as necessary as they are, and they have been referred to in this house-the first thought is for the planting of the seed because that is the seed of life. Surely it is of primary importance to all the people. As I have so often stated, we should not place agriculture in a position

where it is neglected, because upon the welfare of agriculture depends your nation's security; that is your cheapest insurance, to keep agriculture in a prosperous condition.
We all know that agriculture has expanded also in various parts of the country and many agriculturists have done well. We know also that in other areas other forms of agriculture have not done so well. This is the condition that we, as a government, are endeavouring to correct. I am tired, Mr. Speaker, of hearing people, as I sometimes do, refer to the rich farmers. Well, if there are rich farmers they are not in my district. There are some of them who have done better than others, but there are no Cadillacs in my part of the country. The people are glad to have any kind of automobile which they can operate. There are no trips to Florida by the people in my part of the country.
But why should there not be? Why should not farmers have a right to go to Florida and own Cadillacs? This right is given to every other occupation in Canada; every other profession takes that right upon itself. If anyone hears of a farmer having a Cadillac it seems that is an offence against the country, or against nature or against the professions. He has the same right to have a Cadillac but he does not have it. Therefore we would like to suggest that the farmers have expended their greatest efforts to remain in existence, have expended all of their time and all their overtime to make it possible for the people of Canada and of other countries to have food at lower costs than they should have paid.
That is the only reason Canadian farmers are coming to parliament, or to the government, for assistance. They are coming to the government for assistance because over the years the people have paid lower prices for their food than would permit the farmers to continue in farming. What is the alternative? There is no other alternative but for the farmers to come to the government for assistance and to encourage the government to formulate policies that will assist the industry. Why should that be? I ask any person in this House of Commons, why should that be? Why should agriculture ever since I have been associated with it be in the position that it has had to appeal for subsidies and legislation and government operations and so on in order to sustain itself?
Well, the farmers are going to do something about it before the whole economy of the country is completely changed and consider that the economy can get along without agriculture. It is my hope that before that happens the people of this country will be sufficiently sympathetic to make that result possible without the actions that other people 82715-141
The Address-Mr. Studer have it within their power to take to correct their conditions, actions that the farmers do not have within their power. As I mentioned before, with the exception of the larger farmers, who in Canada other than the fishermen have a lower standard of living than the farmer? Yet many things have been done to encourage the farmers and make it possible for them to exist and to make a living comparable with other industries and with other people in Canada.
I have endeavoured to outline the situation in my immediate area, but I do not think it is prevalent everywhere. It may sound like a paradox, but the difficulty in my particular area is that we lack production and have lacked it throughout the years. These people who have overproduction, who have granaries bursting with wheat, who have sufficient credit to carry on and have credit facilities available to them, are in a position where we do not have to worry about them except to help them to sell their grain. We should give our real sympathy to the individual who has not that surplus of grain.
I refer to the ordinary, every-day farmer who is endeavouring to make his living without mining the soil, without taking everything out of the soil and not putting anything back, the small farmer who is trying to make a living for his family and who, by his sweat and toil expended throughout his lifetime, has tried to maintain himself on the land in an effort to supply the people of Canada and other countries with food at below cost. Therefore I would suggest that if we are to remedy that condition, and perhaps it is within our means to partly remedy it, some action should be taken. We are endeavouring, and we shall endeavour, to recommend policies that will bring about that result.
We know the trend in western Canada is toward larger farms. The Gordon commission suggtUed that farms will be still larger in the future, but they will also be more efficient. The same thing will happen as happened in other economies; other provision will have to be made for those who cannot be accommodated within their industry. What this government has endeavoured to do is to have an economy that will absorb those people in whatever occupation of life they may be, be it the forests, the mines or the farms; to absorb them, as it is absorbing them, in other industries in which they can make their living.
No government in the world can guarantee me that I am going to make my living in the profession in which I am working, or the vocation or occupation. The government cannot do that, but it can formulate policies and have an economy that will make it possible

The Address-Mr. Studer for all the people to make their living within whatever form of economy is in existence in the country at the particular time. That is what this government is endeavouring to do.
We are now suggesting to you what the price of food should be. If you were paying the price for food that you should pay, that is the consumers of this country as well as in other countries, then it would not be necessary for the farmers to come to the government for assistance, or to have laws enacted to protect them. If the people of this country and of the world will pay the farmers the price they should receive for the food they produce, then we will not come to the government begging for assistance. I think that is a fair deal.
Why is it that when we go to buy an automobile we do not question the price? They tell us what the price is. We do not haggle over it; we do not argue about it. All things being equal, we either take it or leave it; but when it comes to food we tramp the streets-at least my wife does-looking for the cheapest food. I am trying to train her out of that and to look for the most expensive food, but thus far I have not been successful in doing it. That is the point. When it comes to food we try to get it at the lowest price. In other things, television sets or automobiles, or anything you wish to mention, we ask no questions; we take it home if we have the money.
I would like to suggest to you that the subsidies that are asked for by farmers are merely compensation for the discount the public has received in the price of food throughout the years. If anyone has any other explanation for it, well, I would be glad to hear it. Therefore if you will pay farmers $2.20 let us say, instead of the $1.75 you have been paying during the years from 1944 to 1953, he will not need help. And do not think it is $1.75, because the farmer does not receive that. He receives a maximum of about $1.55, because the $1.75 includes freight; and when the grade is lower, say grade 4, 5 or 6, he receives $1 or less for that wheat. If you will pay $2.20, instead of $1.75 f.o.b. Fort William, which is the fair price he should have been receiving during the past 10 years; instead of 78 cents for oats, 98 cents for oats; instead of $1.16 for barley, $1.45 for barley; instead of $1.95 for rye, $2.45 for rye; instead of $3.65 for flax, $4.59; instead of $18.50 for steers, $23.27; instead of $23.94 for hogs, $30.12; instead of $19.49 for sheep, $24.51; instead of 48 cents for grade A eggs, 57 cents, we will never come here to the House of Commons and ask you for a thing. I think that is a fair

deal. How many bidders do we get on the deal? What do you offer? That is the situation.
Unfortunately, farmers are not in a position where they can demand things as other occupational groups do. We recently had a strike. Even in Saskatchewan, where we have a state-controlled and operated bus system, we had a strike a few years ago. People in Canada have the right to strike if they do not think they are receiving their fair share or a just wage, or for any other cause. But how can the farmer strike? He cannot do a thing about it. He can have his unions, and then through political agitation or some other type of agitation they disappear. That has been proven in the past, and the farmers have no one to speak for them except their representatives in the House of Commons, the grass roots representatives who come from Saskatchewan, and by those I mean the Liberal representatives because the other groups from the province of Saskatchewan who are supposed to represent the farmers are not the grass roots; they are the quack grass roots.
I would suggest to the people of western Canada that it is the real grass roots that produce something in abundance, that produce the revenue for the farmers. In other words they are the people who are listened to. The proof that the people of Canada have not been listening to Saskatchewan is the fact that the majority of the representatives from Saskatchewan during the past few years have not been true representatives of the people. In other words they are the enemies of the government, and if the government represents the people of Canada, then they must be the enemies of the people. At least that is the way it looks to me. If the people of western Canada wish to have representation that would be of value here in eastern Canada and in this parliament, they should do something about it.
The government has been doing something about it. Instead of having our farm unions come here to present their case, the representatives of the people have been trying to do it here in this house. I would suggest that any time the farmers of western Canada do not think that their representatives have been doing it sufficiently well they should themselves come here to Ottawa. They have the same right as anyone else to come here. We have seen people from different organizations who thought they had a grievance walk up and down in front of the House of Commons. The farmers have the same right; why should they not have it? This government is as partial and sympathetic to them as to anyone else; therefore I would advise

The Address-Mr. Studer
them to come whenever they think they can make an appeal to the government that will be more effective, and whenever they have any wrong they think should be corrected. They can present it to their own seat of government, and they have the same right to do so as the people in any democratic country.
The government has been endeavouring to correct the difficulties existing among the farmers. The government has made operative policies to stabilize agriculture and to encourage co-operatives. Incidentally, I might say there is no problem for which farmers cannot find a solution in their co-operatives. In fact they could get along fairly well even without representatives because they have the solution right in their own hands, providing someone does not disturb the cooperatives. Throughout the years the farmers have been able to solve their own difficulties through the co-operatives. The federal government has encouraged co-operatives, as did the former government in Saskatchewan and as the present one in turn is doing. In their efforts to assist the farmers the federal government has operated a wheat board on behalf of the farmers of western Canada, and has taken it upon itself not only to promote the wheat board but to extend it for five years. It has supported the international wheat agreements and provided loans to foreign countries to purchase Canadian grain. It has also instituted floor prices on wheat, oats, barley, hogs, butter and eggs. It has originated the Agricultural Prices Support Act, the Agricultural Products Marketing Act, and has paid out over $1 billion in subsidies to farmers in the past decade as has been pointed out in an issue of the Western Producer printed in Saskatoon a year or two ago. It has made the Canadian farm loan board operative and promoted the P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A., and it is now thinking of crop insurance as far as it is applicable to western Canada. It has also progressively abolished tariffs and removed the duty on farm machinery and supplies. It has negotiated trade agreements with 73 countries of the world.
Why have these considerations been necessary? They have been necessary for the reason I stated at the beginning of my remarks, because the public has been paying less than the cost of production to the farmers of western Canada, and there is no alternative except to have the government promote, advocate and originate policies that will compensate the farmers for the difference between what they actually receive and what they really should receive, something that will help meet what the price should have been in the first place. Agriculture
has to be supported because circumstances over which it has no control prevent it from sustaining itself.
What are the demands of farmers today? They demand policies that will enable them to produce without government assistance, and that is a reasonable request. The farmers ask, how high can floor prices be advanced without instituting production controls? No one has ever given them an answer. The farmers are also asking, can a parity price be established without acreage control? No one in this House of Commons has answered that question. The only body to have answered it is the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The vice president of the wheat pool said that if you instituted parity prices as promulgated or formulated by certain farm organizations, then you would have to establish it at between 65 and 85 per cent of parity or the farmers would go hog wild on production.
If the farmers want parity prices under which to reduce their acreage to the extent of the wheat that can be absorbed in this country-because you cannot expect the 16 million people in Canada to pay the difference -they should have the right to vote for that, and we will give them consideration on that basis. If they wish to produce one hog instead of three to come under a parity price structure they should have the right to vote on that.
However, they must also take into consideration that by doing so they will be reducing the entire economy of Canada, the gross national product of the country, because if you reduce your acreage and production from 500 million to 150 million bushels then Canada has lost the difference between the value to be received from the 150 million and the revenue to be received from 500 million, and perhaps that is not in the best interests of the national economy. For this reason the farmers will not vote for parity prices under that system, but they have a right to express their opinion through a vote on control and acreage reductions, the same as a union has the right to express its opinion concerning whether or not a strike vote should be taken.
I would therefore suggest to the farmers that policies be originated which are acceptable to the rest of the people of Canada, including the members of this house; because if they cannot accept them then they are wasting their time. The recommendations of the Gordon commission concerning wheat are in the public eye at the moment. These could be considered, if the farmers would accept the consequences and dangers particularly as

The Address-Mr. Siuder they relate to the wheat board, the economy of Canada and their own economy.
What the farmers want are stabilized prices for their production. They want crop insurance for those years when there are no crops. They want unemployment insurance to be extended to farm labour, and they want every effort to be expended in an effort to sell their produce. They want more storage for their grain and equalized freight rates so they are not penalized because of where they live.
Incidentally, if this can be thrown in, I might point out that farmers want the other amenities of life which are enjoyed by approximately 75 per cent of the people of Canada. In other words, in our part of the country in order to keep up to date I think we should have some of the modern conveniences and pleasures of life. We in the southwest also want a television station so we can enjoy the educational benefits of programs and in order that the cultural advantages television provides to the other people in Canada will not pass us by. The farmers want no more and no less than the same security and standard of living enjoyed by those in other occupations.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we commend the government for having created an economy that can absorb those whom agriculture cannot accommodate.
I would point out, however, that not all our troubles are due to circumstances such as I have described. Some of our troubles in the west are due to politics, and I would like to dwell on that subject for a moment because if there is any place in Canada where political disunity exists and has existed throughout the years with harmful effects it is among the farmers in western Canada. There is an old saying to the effect that united we stand and divided we fall. Well, if we in western Canada have fallen it has been through division, it has been through political disunity, and it has been because individuals have proclaimed that their election was more important than the welfare of western Canada.
During the last 30 years have we not had an example of the futility of divided strength, when splinter political parties say, "Elect me and I will correct the difficulties that exist in western Canada." It is interesting to note that none of the difficulties have been corrected, at least according to what the disunited opposition members of parliament tell us. They constantly tell us that nothing has been accomplished as a result of their efforts. They bemoan the fact that they have been here year after year telling the


government what should be done, and nothing has happened as a result of their pleas. I can only observe that they must have made an extremely poor job of it if they have been unable to convince any other person in the whole of the country that the situation in western Canada is as they have described it. I suggest to them that they go back home and tell the people there that they have been a complete failure in representing western Canada. They have gone among the people there and suggested that fighters be sent here; that is what they told them.

speechtext:
Well, if they are fighters and if they have fought for something, where is it? They point out in every speech they make that they have been unable to accomplish anything for western Canada. A prime example is the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), the "Quebec is ripe for communism" member from Burnaby-Coquitlam. He was a pathetic example as he stood in the House of Commons just two days ago and wept over the plight of the people in his constituency. He does not need to weep; he merely needs to be told to go back to his constituency and tell the people there to send a representative to the parliament of Canada who will speak on behalf of his people and who will be believed by the rest of the people of Canada.
So far he has not done so. So far none of the others have done so. There is no sense in my standing here weeping floods of tears over the plight of the old age pensioners if it does not cost me anything. If I have never produced a single nickel's worth of wealth in the world it is easy for me to ask other people to make their contributions. I would suggest to them that if they produced some wealth to distribute for the benefit and welfare of the people of Canada instead of teaching the children of Canada socialism in their schools, it would be better for us all. Because that is what they have been doing, teaching socialism to the children in western Canada; and if they have not been doing so they have not been doing their duty as socialists.
So, Mr. Speaker, all our difficulties are not due to climatic conditions or to the policies of the government. I was interested the other day in hearing the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) try to explain the difference between Social Credit and socialist credit, and I would suggest to him that his explanation why there is Social Credit is not genuine. The reason there is Social Credit is that 50, 60 or 70 per cent of the Social

Credit members here sit under that title because they were not qualified to be Liberal candidates at previous elections, and in order to be elected to the House of Commons they formulated the hodge-podge of discarded political theories that all the civilizations in the world threw away long ago. They have been playing with the discards out of the deck for so many years that they do not know what a new deck is. They have been playing neulo with the discards and there are no face cards in the discards; all the face cards are on the government side of the house. They are relegated to playing neulo in this political game. They are a party of Rosicrucian technocrats with hellfire and brimstone and applesauce; with a policy that was spawned in some other country and which grew to maturity, if you could ever call it that, in the foothills of Alberta. What a discredited organization they are. Did you read the recent Commission's report in New Zealand, where there was a Social Credit government of what Social Credit is?
They claim they have a monopoly of political righteousness. Without referring to any individual I would say they have a monopoly of hypocrisy, because they originated politics and in doing so they caused all areas of western Canada to suffer for the sake of their political expediency. They are the jokesters of the House of Commons and, Mr. Speaker, though I could use some other words, I would just like to ask where is the $25 they were supposed to have had in Alberta as a result of the Aberhart administration. The people of Alberta got it, but not from the Social Credit organization. They got it from the Liberals. They got it from the Liberals through family allowances, through the same organization and the same policies every one of them had voted against to defeat the government on February 10, 1944.
It was a sin against humanity to deprive the mothers of western Canada of these family allowance benefits by trying to defeat the government on a policy of that kind. Even the Conservatives had the good sense not to do this. The Social Crediters should go out in western Canada and confess their sins and tell the people about the crimes they have committed in the name of humanity. Instead they imagine that they have a halo and that they have a dispensation to promote socialist credit throughout the country. That would destroy this country as quickly as socialism, because the whole policy is dependent on state control. I challenge them to deny it, these so-called professors of freedom.

The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) or for some other constituency was telling us that Major Douglas, who invented socialist credit, came out to Alberta and disappeared overnight. Why? The hon. member explained that he went because he had a difference of opinion with the Premier of Alberta. That is not why he went. When the sterilization laws came into existence, or anticipating them, he knew what was good for him.
I suggest that when socialist credit comes into existence it will not be necessary, because there will be no people left in Canada. Even I would go-head for the ocean and swim for it if I had to-as Major Douglas would, before I would place myself under the jurisdiction of such a sterilization law. I understand that the insane people would be affected by it, and that a board would be set up. But how can the blind lead the blind? How can a lunatic determine who is sane? No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we want social or socialist credit in this country. I would suggest to the members of that party that they were originally Liberals in Alberta, and that they should come back to the fold and make a contribution to the welfare of the people of Canada.
We have, also, some remnants of the socialist party left in Saskatchewan. If they are not a disillusioned party no one has ever been disillusioned. They heaped abuse upon the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) because he left the party, but he was merely a precursor of the inevitable, a St. John the Baptist; because, following him, in September or October they all gathered in Winnipeg.
What was the result? At the same time the communists were tearing down Stalin the socialists at Winnipeg were taking the ground from under Karl Marx. What have they left? The Liberal policy. Therefore I suggest to them that they should leave their policy, forget all about their particular theories which make no contribution to the welfare of Canada, and associate themselves with the new, growing and great Conservative

It is always necessary when you have leaders to have a few followers, and there has been no dearth of leaders in the Conservative party. speechtext:
We in Bruce
county are very proud of the fact that our leader has such strong ties with us, and that his mother is a Bruce county girl. The last resting place of two of his grandparents is to be found in a beautiful rustic setting in the cemetery at Tiverton, nine miles from my home town of Kincardine.
[Mr. Studer.l

It is my happy lot, Mr. Speaker, to be chosen to represent the good people of Bruce county in the House of Commons. When I say "good people" I mean it in every sense of the word. They are mostly descendants of pioneers who settled there 100 or more years ago. The names of these pioneers have passed down from generation to generation. If you will pardon a personal note, I wish to say that our son is the fourth generation on the farm that my grandfather operated over 100 years ago. In addition to the descendants of these early pioneers we have many people who have chosen Bruce as an ideal place in which to live and raise a family.
Bruce county is well up to the top in production of dairy products, beef and hogs in the province of Ontario. Bruce county, as I have stated before, has approximately 300 miles of shoreline bordering on the blue waters of lake Huron and Georgian bay. We have an ever-growing business in summer visitors, both from Canada and the United States of America. Many visitors, after experiencing the friendly atmosphere of our people and seeing the beautiful sunsets over lake Huron, which are known over the world, decide at once that they wish to come back every summer for their vacation.
We have many nice towns and villages in Bruce, all ideal places for anyone to live. We have good schools, good churches, good stores and good roads. Some of the towns and villages have industries, some large and some small. Many of these industries have been located in Bruce for a great number of years, while a few are of more recent growth.
Irrespective of the facts I have given concerning Bruce, there is a growing discontent among the citizens. The farmers are in the squeeze between falling farm prices and the ever-increasing cost of production. Because of the increased size of farms due to mechanization, their sons and daughters must leave home to find jobs, mostly in the cities. In some of our towns and villages we have factory buildings that are closed. Over the last decade the population of Canada has increased rapidly, but Bruce county has not shared in that increase.
According to the preliminary report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects it is expected that Canada's population will reach 26 million in 1980. On page 66, paragraph 11, these words are to be found:
It seems probable that the demand for secondary manufacturers will be at about the same rate as the anticipated increase in the gross national product. In this event the total demand by 1980 may be three times what it is at present.

The question here arises, is Bruce county going to get its share of that secondary manufacturing increase? On page 3, paragraph 7, of the Gordon report you will find these words:
Throughout our work we have made a number of general assumptions on which all our forecasts are predicated. Of overriding significance in the world today is the fact that two great powers, the United States and the Soviet union, both possess weapons of mass destruction in such quantity that their use might destroy organized society throughout the world. Other countries may well acquire an armament of similarly frightening power before many years are over, and this would add to the potential danger. Within a few years intercontinental missiles with nuclear warheads will be in existence, capable at a single blow of crippling, if not completely destroying, any city, no matter how large. A single hydrogen weapon, for example, could devastate and make uninhabitable an area approximately 50 miles wide and 200 miles long. Such an area, stretching along the shores of lake Ontario, might extend from Hamilton at one end to Kingston at the other, and include within its orbit Toronto, Oshawa, Port Hope and Belleville. A similar area along the St. Lawrence might run from the Ontario-Quebee border to Quebec city and contaminate with radioactive fall-out all the cities, towns and villages in between, including the entire population of Montreal. These are among the new facts of life and death in this nuclear age.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that this in itself is reason enough for all governments to encourage decentralization of industry. On February 21, 1956, civil defence co-ordinator F. F. Worthington had this to say in Belleville, Ontario:
If I were a dictator in this country I would ban cities of more than 50,000 population and order Toronto and Montreal to stop growing.
Mr. Worthington said the expense of decentralization was nothing compared to saving lives of people or the life of the country. Sweden, he said, was limiting cities to 25,000 population. There are many ways and means of encouraging decentralization rather than by direct orders of any dictator. The report of a special committee of the Ontario legislature on air pollution and smoke control was tabled on March 15, 1956, by the chairman, A. H. Cowling. It had this to say in part:
It Is estimated that smoke and smog in their various forms cost the people of this province about $120 million a year. It is also a fact that air pollution does have a detrimental effect on the physical and mental health, the efficiency and wellbeing of people who must exist in it.
Air pollution affects every citizen, the report states. Depending upon his activity, each individual inhales from 8,000 to 16,000 quarts of air per day. Great attention is being paid to the purity of food and water supplies, but very little has been done yet about the vital air supply.
For generations, we have been content to inhale several thousand gallons of contaminated air every day.
The Address-Mr. A. E. Robinson
Air, like water, is a limited natural resource. It has taken us a long time to realize that there is a limit to the amount of man's garbage the air can absorb and still be suitable for living in. We have come to the conclusion that air pollution is a serious, dangerous and costly curse to civilized living.
Industrial areas, of course, are the most affected. In this respect the air pollution problem is most serious in Toronto, where it is estimated to cost people of the area at least $60 million a year. Based on studies made in the United States and the United Kingdom, the report estimates that polluted air costs every person in the Toronto area an average of $40 a year, and that the average cost per person across Ontario is in excess of $20 a year.
The old-fashioned idea was that a smoking chimney is a sign of full lunch pails and of prosperity.
So states the report. It continues:
Today, however, it is an indication of waste, of bad manners, and of a source of unnecessary dirt and work for the housewife.
It may also be a sign of full hospital beds. Air pollution does have a detrimental effect on the physical and mental health, the efficiency and wellbeing of people who must exist in it.
There is considerable evidence to indicate that it is one of the causes for the growing incidence of lung cancer.
It certainly predisposes the Individual to other respiratory illnesses and to cardiac trouble, and makes his recovery protracted, or his complaint chronic.
It can cause sudden death and has produced many episodes throughout the world which have resulted in large numbers of fatalities.
On the other hand, deaths from cancer of the trachea, lung and bronchus, from cancer of all kinds and from pneumonia and bronchitis are unexpectedly low in the rural areas and in Ontario municipalities with population less than 15,000.
The London Free Press in an editorial dated May 12, 1955, had this to say:
Too much concentration in a few larger cities will make for a situation such as in Australia, where nearly half the population is to be found in a few great cities. It has not been a healthy development. This must be avoided if at all possible in Ontario and in Canada.
J. V. McAree, a noted columnist, writing in the Globe and Mail, had this to say about traffic congestion in Toronto:
To wait fifteen minutes or more while crowded cars go by is a daily experience to tens of thousands. But we think that instead of blaming the Toronto transport commission, we in Toronto should realize that we are paying a price for living in a metropolitan city. What we are suffering every person in a big city suffers. There is no escape from it except possibly to move to a smaller town.
Mr. Speaker, I do not say that any government should force an industry to locate in any certain area, but I do say very emphatically that provincial and federal governments should encourage the decentralization of industry by improving the services which they,

The Address-Mr. Girard the governments, are responsible for, such as transportation facilities by road, water and rail, and cheaper electric power for outlying districts. I hope the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, considers well the resolution that was passed at the annual convention of the Ontario municipal electrical association held in Toronto early in 1956. That resolution asked the commission to consider taking steps that would eventually lead to an equalization of wholesale power rates to all municipalities in the province.
Mr. Speaker, concerning transportation by water, I wish to state that we in Bruce county have many locations where harbour facilities are crying for attention. Money is spent occasionally in small amounts, mostly for repairs, and in some cases the money spent does not bring any benefit whatsoever. As I stated before, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Transport should get together to formulate a plan of long-term improvements. By doing so they would save much of the money that is now being spent foolishly.
To the Minister of Transport I wish to say that the railway situation in Bruce is, to say the least, unsatisfactory. Down through the years the hard-working, industrious citizens of Bruce have paid their share of the C.N.R. deficits and in return received poorer and poorer service. Owing to this poorer service some business to the rail lines was lost, and of late years the C.N.R. has talked of curtailing the service we now have. I plead with the Minister of Transport to see that we not only hold the service we have but in addition receive improved service. It will be a sorrowful day if the good citizens of Bruce continue to be sacrificed on the altar of centralization.
As the Minister of Finance has the privilege of representing part of Bruce county, I feel that I am quite in order in drawing to his attention our hopes for a brighter industrial future.
I am very sorry that the Gordon commission did not recognize the seriousness of the problem of centralization, as I am sure there are many other districts with problems similar to those we have in Bruce. I am also disappointed that the throne speech did not deal more with health insurance, increased pensions to the aged and needy, the blind and the veterans. These increases are due owing to the higher cost of living and inflation, and they will probably be produced before the next election as election propaganda.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to acknowledge the principle of bilingualism in the house I should like


to say a few words in the English language. First may I extend my compliments to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. May I extend the compliments of the season to all the members of the house. I should like to wish a victorious come-back to all members after the next election, but we must let the interests of the nation come first. Hence I shall leave the choice to Providence.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the recent C.P.R. strike has again given rise to the grave worries that beset the minds of all every time we witness a labour dispute of some importance.
We might even say that if labour problems are of concern to the public at large, it is more because those problems are a threat to people's comfort than because people are anxious to work efficiently for the establishment of true social justice. Politicians in particular work hard to preserve the sympathy of the workers but it is apparent that the politician fears the worker more than he understands him. There is promotion of economic liberalism in all its forms; the virtues of private enterprise are rightfully extolled but we forget to give it a heart. We are afraid to see the worker throw himself into a dangerous socialism which often leads to communism, but we forget that capital, which is heartless, is one of the main causes responsible for that threat. Economic liberalism, which is based on the inexorable law of supply and demand, leads to competition. In the face of this taskmaster, the only course open to the worker is the labour union, whose main force resides in the threat to strike. If ever the day comes when workers will no longer have the right to strike, we shall no longer have democracy.
Whether or not some strikes are just, whether or not they serve the ambitions of some individuals, it is not up to us here to decide. However, we who are responsible for the commonweal have a duty to improve the social climate that brings about these strikes. Every finished product coming out of a factory is the fruit of the harmonious union of two main factors, namely capital and labour.
In the social field, instead of close cooperation between capital and labour, we have a conflict of two groups from which originate misunderstandings between the main parties as they both remain obstinately attached to their own particular ideas, as well as misunderstandings among other groups of anxious bystanders who measure the repercussions of these disputes by the

yardstick of their own interests. There is great talk of rights but little or no talk of obligations. Let capital have compassion and help the worker lose his own rancour. In his Magna Carta of labour, the encyclical Quadragesimo Anno, the text quoted being from page 140, Five Great Encyclicals, the Paulist Press, 1945, Pius XI has clearly defined the role of capital and labour. He declares among other things in this encyclical:
It is therefore entirely false to ascribe the results of their combined efforts to either party alone: and it is flagrantly unjust that either should deny the efficacy of the other and seize all the profits.
This encyclical which is the social gospel of right-thinking conservatives nonetheless recognizes the right of capital to a reasonable profit but also claims for the worker a family salary which takes into account both the cost of living and of services rendered. This is where, to my mind, the state should intervene to protect the family which is the basic cell of society. A family allowance proportionate to the number of children must restore the family budget. It is a fact that the same salary for the same work can at once be a reasonable salary for a bachelor and the small family and a totally inadequate one for the father of a large family.
It is true that the multiplication of social measures leads to state socialism, but some are indispensable for the preservation of a social balance, and family allowances are, to my mind, the most essential legislation.
Immigration is called upon to people our country, whereas we should preach a higher birthrate which would enable the large family to prosper as it should. The hon. Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) has said and rightly that he had greater confidence in Canadian babies than in immigrants for peopling our country. I hope he will draw the logical conclusion of his convictions and agree to a raise in family allowances, which is essential if Canadian babies are to multiply. I have asked every year in this house and I am insisting upon it again-that the government make family allowances proportionate to the cost of living. If a minimum rate of $5 was thought absolutely necessary in 1945 for this allowance, why do we tolerate that it should fall to $3.25 in 1957, as a result of the constant rise of living costs?
On every occasion when we advocated an increase of family allowances, we have been met with an easy answer about the lack of money.
When the time comes to appropriate billions of dollars for national defence, for the Colombo plan, for our contributions to NATO,
The Address-Mr. Herridge and for some justifiable assistance to the Hungarian people, the government is softhearted. However, when the family is at stake, financial considerations are uppermost in its mind.
With the $400 million surplus of this year's budget, added to the $22 million we are about to dispose of as a free gift, family allowances could be doubled for the next ten years without an increase of a single cent in taxes. We are fed up with the financial argument. This government is far too generous in the fields assigned exclusively to the provinces by our constitution to act as a poor relation when the vital interests of the family are at stake.
I hope that the government will change the Family Allowances Act so that the allowance may be paid for dependent students as long as they are going on with their studies. I hope also that the government will do away with the inconsistent law which allows the deduction of only $150 to parents whose children receive the allowance. This is levying a tax on social legislation itself and take back with one hand what is given by the other. This money comes from taxes and to tax it is to levy a tax on a tax.
Let us place the family first. We will thus discharge our duties more surely and thus contribute to remove the dangers which threaten our world.
On the international level, in every country, in the heart of every human society and in the individual himself, we find the same universal "sore"; the world is dying from a lack of generosity. If we were as keen about charity as we are about our rights, the world would not need so many guns.

There are many things in the throne speech, Mr. Speaker, that indicate the government proposes to introduce legislation that we welcome, such as the establishment of the Canada Council, the implication that there are going to be increased grants to universities, and the suggestion that a committee of the Senate be established to deal with conservation and the development of agricultural land in Canada. While these things are commendable and are welcomed by us, we find on an examination of the throne speech that there is a complete lack of proposals for the introduction of legislation that will meet the needs of many Canadians who require assistance and consideration at this time.
I have been searching for a reason, Mr. Speaker, as to why the throne speech is so barren of this legislation that most of us had

The Address-Mr. Herridge a right to expect and which I think a good many of the Canadian people were expecting. I think I have come to the correct conclusion. I have come to the opinion that the government considers the official opposition no menace to its continued existence, and on that account we have this address with rather scanty proposals for legislation at this session.
I sympathize sincerely with the opposition, which contains a group of men of unquestioned integrity, many of them good friends of ours, genial and hard-working. But in the present circumstances in Canada they operate under a very severe handicap. I would say that they are a group of gentlemen who are frustrated in their efforts to do good by the strait-jacket of the circumstances that exist in Canada today.
If they adopt concrete proposals that go to the right, they lose popular support. If they develop some concrete proposals that go to the left, they find themselves in our camp. They are, therefore, in very difficult circumstances. Generally speaking I believe that is the reason they find it necessary to sit on the fence on most major issues, and to date have not proposed an alternative program. As our leader said some days ago, you cannot suggest to the Canadian people that you are an alternative to the present government unless you have an alternative program. I sympathize with them because it is most difficult for them to provide an alternative program to the program of the government of the day.
I said that was why they were reduced to sitting on the fence on risky and major issues. It was for that reason their leader did not take a definite stand on the strike issue. It is for that reason they are constantly required to speak in ambiguous terms. They cannot help it; the circumstances in Canada force that upon them. It is for that reason their major policy at the moment is one of directing questions to the cabinet on the orders of the day on matters, on many occasions, of little consequence.
I do not blame these hon. gentlemen for that approach. They are confined to that approach by the fact that the Progressive Conservative party, under the conditions that exist in Canada at this time, is a species that will be extinct in 10 years. I feel sorry for these gentlemen because some of them are good members. I may say the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) would make a good member of this group with a little polishing up on economics. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) would be a welcome addition. He is considered by some a secret C.C.F.'er. There are a number of other members in the group whose objectives

in broad outline are the same as ours or those of any other hon. member who wishes to represent the people and see some improvement in Canadian conditions; that is, they wish to do well by the Canadian people, but-

It is for that reason I say that the situation in Canada is developing under which this group offers an alternative policy to that of the government in power. We have a different basic philosophy and we have concrete proposals to put before the house and the country, namely democratic socialism.
I will admit that the party has a new leader, who no doubt will do his best. Mind you, they have a certain advantage over us in that respect, because the new leader of the Progressive Conservative party is a master of propaganda. His public relations organization, which has constant contacts with the press; his knowledge of the use of the radio and photographs at home, when they are appropriate, are such-and I admit it-that if the Leader of the Opposition were to burp tomorrow in the outer recesses of Afghanistan it would be known around the world in 24 hours. Mr. Speaker, under present conditions that will not elect a party that finds it impossible to produce an alternative program to that of the Liberal party at this time.
I say we have an alternative program. Our fundamental objective in Canada at this time is the development and conservation of our human and natural resources. We see this problem as a whole. I cannot deal at length with our program tonight to indicate that we do have a basic program in opposition to the government in power. We believe that under present economic and social conditions in Canada we have to look at our problems as a whole from a national point of view. That is why we believe in basic planning. We believe in the enlargement of the sector of public ownership in this country. We believe that a great number of these developments will not be undertaken to the advantage of the Canadian people unless they are at least promoted and developed as a result of federal government co-operation with the provincial governments

concerned, whether it is development in the maritimes, the building of the South Saskatchewan dam or the building of the necessary dams in the development of the Columbia.
