In addition to that we believe in genuine free enterprise. We believe in providing opportunities for legitimate competitive free enterprise and for the development and extension of co-operative ownership in this country. We believe in the use of Canadian capital for the development of Canadian natural resources. We believe we have a program that would make this possible under present conditions, and make it unnecessary to bring into this country such large imports of United States and other capital at this time. We believe in a national development investment board for that purpose, so that investment could be directed to the best social advantage. We believe in a national investment and development bank.
We believe that if the federal government used its powers in relation to the use of the national credit and mobilized the national savings under a national investment board, whether they are corporate or personal, we could do a great deal to build these things which are required in Canada with Canadian savings and resources. In addition we believe it is very necessary that there should be a revision of special exemptions to corporations, and we also believe there must be an increase in corporation taxes and higher income taxes. We say that frankly. We do not believe in making proposals for social welfare improvements without at the same time coming out frankly and saying we have to get the money to do these things, and we suggest where we should get it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned the possibilities in the revision of exemptions given to corporations in Canada at the present time and the possibilities in higher income taxes. In support of that argument I wish to read briefly some figures which have been obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics and the Bank of Canada. When these figures are given let no one say that we cannot consider the needs of old age pensioners, disability pensioners and others in the country at this time. Between 1946 and 1955 there was a total of $6,940 million in undistributed corporate profits in Canada. In addition, between 1946 and 1955 the total depreciation allowances permitted corporations amounted to $11,214 million, and the total of corporation internally-generated funds amounted to
The Address-Mr. Herridge $1,854 million. During that same period we had a net direct foreign investment in Canada of $2,119 million.
We are all concerned about the cost of living, and without doubt the cost of living is caused primarily by the excessive amount of direct foreign investment in Canada and competition for materials and labour. It is almost a direct result of heavy investment spending. I suggest in that connection our fiscal policies are radically different from those of the government. They are possibly policies that the official opposition would not advance, because they do not believe in taking this sort of action. Therefore under these circumstances we suggest there can be a legitimate increase in corporation taxes and higher income taxes, and there should be a revision of corporate exemptions. From these two sources we would obtain tremendous assets to give effect to some of the things we propose.
We now come to the cost -of living. The government to date has a restricted money policy. I want to bring to the attention of the house an article that I happened to be reading this, evening. It will be found in the January 19 issue of Saturday Night. Apparently the Minister of National Revenue recently addressed a meeting in Toronto with respect to this question. This is what the article has to say with reference to the minister's remarks:
Dr. McCann could have given the students something better to think about by discussing, not the inevitability of tight money in inflationary times, but the relationship of economic development, inflation and credit controls that are not selective.
Credit restraint that is non-selective, however, is a clumsy, perhaps even a dangerous weapon against inflation. It has proved to be far from the delicate mechanism that economists talked about a few years ago.
When there is too much demand for too little money, the available funds flow inevitably into the most profitable channels.
That is our objection to the present credit controls. The article goes on:
More often than not, the most profitable uses of money are also the most productive ones, from a business viewpoint. But while productive, these may not be the most imperative social uses. Unable to borrow, for example, builders are unable to put up as many houses and buyers must take on the extra load of higher interest rates; municipalities must either delay building the schools and other services they need or shoulder a heavier burden of debt.
If credit must be controlled, it seems necessary that it also be rationed. Dr. McCann and his colleagues should do some serious thinking about credit in terms of distribution as well as restriction.
Personally I think those are extremely sound observations. Our credit restrictions should not be such as to prevent the building of houses, the provision of services required by municipalities, or those things that are

The Address-Mr. Herridge required socially at this time. Our credit restrictions should be such that those projects do not suffer from whatever credit restrictions are necessary. It is because we take this point of view that we believe we are sound in urging the program we present to this house and to the country.
We have heard a great deal about prosperity, and without a doubt there is a general measure of prosperity in Canada at the present time, and there has been for some years; but there are many Canadians who at this moment do not enjoy that prosperity, and those Canadians are overlooked in the proposals contained in the throne speech. Because we believe our fiscal policies are alternative policies to those of the government and that they are sound because they are based on the theory that two and two make four, we say certain things can be done by this government to meet the needs of the people of this country at this time.
It is for that'reason we advocate increased old age security, increased old age assistance and a reduction of the qualification age. We realize this would cost the country more money, but on the basis of the corporate profits paid out during the last 10 years, on the basis of the undistributed dividends, on the basis of total exemptions of corporations and on the basis of over $2 billion being spent for defence, surely no one could reasonably argue that if we sit down and try to redistribute the wealth of this country at this time in such a manner as to give all fair shares, we cannot do what is necessary for our older citizens. We say that if we want to we can give them $75 a month without question.
In that connection I also want to bring to the attention of the house what I consider an injustice. Judges, civil servants and other persons who receive various types of pensions from the federal government are allowed to leave Canada and continue to receive their pensions. In the case of persons receiving old age security or assistance they can leave Canada only for a period of three months. If they are not away for a longer period than three months I understand they are able to collect their cheques covering the period they were absent, but for not more than three months in any one year.
Surely these senior citizens who pioneered in this country have as much right to go to California or to the south in the winter because of their health or in order to overcome severe climatic conditions that exist in their districts as have judges and other federal pensioners, I think that is most unjust, and I urge the government when it introduces the measure to increase old age pensions to


give consideration to permitting old age pensioners to enjoy the same rights with respect to leaving Canada as are enjoyed by other pensioners of the federal government.
Because of our belief in our sound fiscal policies simply through a proper redistribution of the wealth that now exists, we continue to urge a national health insurance plan, not a hospital plan but a total health insurance plan that will provide for hospital services, medical attention, drugs and the other clinical services that are necessary at this time.
We also continue to urge, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did the other day, the necessity for a national industrial pension scheme. I brought this up in the house at the last two sessions, and I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South has mentioned it for 10 years in succession to my knowledge. This is a scheme that requires only government administration and coordination. It will cost the government very little more than at present. We ask the government to give consideration to establishing a national industrial pension scheme so the workers employed in various industries in this country will have freedom of movement in labour, will be able to go from one plant to another instead of being chained to one plant by any present pension scheme after paying for more than five years because of the fear of losing their pension rights and so on.
We believe there should be greater provision for low cost housing. That will cost the government some money. I shall not deal with it at length at this time, but we in this group see no reason at all why we should not be giving these benefits to needy Canadians on the basis of the gross production of the country.
I want to refer briefly to the Legion brief which was presented to the cabinet by the dominion officers of the Legion on November 9. We all know the Canadian Legion and the other senior veterans associations are responsible organizations who are in touch with conditions as they concern veterans across this country through provincial commands, zones and local branches. I am pleased to see, Mr. Speaker, that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs is listening intently to what I have to say.
The Legion brief dealt largely with suggested amendments to the Pension Act and to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I believe the Legion representatives presented excellent arguments and evidence in the brief, and it is my opinion that the veterans affairs committee should be established immediately

to give consideration to these representations from the Canadian Legion and other bodies. In fact, it is the opinion of this group that the veterans affairs committee should be a permanent committee.
I do not intend to deal at length with this brief. I support the proposals because I have read the brief. I know the circumstances they refer to, and I believe their requests are fair, sound and within the capacity of the Canadian people to meet financially.
In their representations the Legion urge that section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that where a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of war is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or a disease not recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or had its inception subsequent to enlistment. I know that is a difficult question, but the number of veterans affected by this amendment would be relatively small, and I urge the government to give consideration to this proposal because there is an injustice done to some veterans under the present legislation.
The Legion also urges revision of the rates for dependent parents, and recommends that the pension of dependent parents be restored to the former position whereby the rate for one parent was equal to the rate for a widow, with a more adequate additional amount than at present provided where there are two dependent parents. I know the parliamentary assistant realizes this is a recurring problem for the Canadian pension commission and those responsible for the administration of this act. The Legion then asks for an increased pension to certain dependent parents, and recommends that section 38 of the Pension Act be amended so that a dependent parent of a deceased member of the forces would become eligible for the maximum rate on the remarriage of the pensioned widow, even though pension is still being paid on account of a child or children of the deceased serviceman.
There is a further resolution here that I am not at all surprised to see in which they recommend that all disability pensions when granted should become effective from the date of application; but in order to allay fears of excessive awards going back to the first world war, jeopardizing the chances of the applicant, they append the following saving clause, namely that this provision should not apply to claims granted prior to January 1, 1946 and that no retroactive payments shall be made for a period prior to that date. I think that is a very reasonable
The Address-Mr. Herridge and modest request as a result of my experience with the operation of that section of the act at the present time.
They also recommend that in order to obviate all possibility of future diversion of war pensions, section 24(3) of the act be amended to bind the Crown specifically so that a pension cannot be attached in any circumstances.
Then they come to the veterans who served in the first world war in the United Kingdom, and who are presently denied certain rights. They recommend that these veterans who saw service in the United Kingdom or with other allied governments should be brought within the provisions of section 13 of the act in the same way as those who were in Newfoundland at the time of enlistment.
Later they go on to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I give credit to the government that the later amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act brought great benefits to many veterans, and I know from personal knowledge that they have been appreciated by many people who were able to take advantage of those amendments. I raise this point because our legislation has, generally speaking, been good. These are recommendations by the Canadian Legion as a result of their experience in the administration of these acts in recent years. In the light of this experience the Canadian Legion has recommended that ceilings on total permissible incomes under the War Veterans' Allowance Act be increased to $1,200 per year for the single recipient and $2,000 per year for the married recipient. The Legion also recommends that the married rate of war veterans allowance be increased from $108 per month to $120 a month. That was the point of major dispute when the act was before the veterans affairs committee some two or three years ago.
Further, the Legion recommends that Canadian veterans of the first world war whose overseas service was restricted to the United Kingdom be eligible for war veterans allowance provided that such service be at least one year in duration. That clause "one year in duration" has been added, very sensibly I think because at times there is evidence that the veteran was posted to Great Britain on service, frequently against his will. There are very few of these veterans who served in England in the first world war alive today, and the granting of this request of the Canadian Legion would not mean a very large expenditure on the part of the government. I would urge that further consideration be given to this question.

The Address-Mr. Herridge
Later they come to the question of the widows of allied ex-servicemen and urge that they be granted war veterans allowances where the recipient died before completing 20 years' residence in Canada, providing:
(a)	That the effective date of her eligibility be 20 years after the husband's arrival to take up permanent residence in Canada;
(b)	That the widow herself has completed 20 years' residence in Canada, and
(c)	That the husband and wife were both otherwise eligible.
There follows another clause which I think is a very necessary amendment to the act, and that is the recommendation which deals with the permissible equity in the value of the house which a veteran may own. The present figure is $6,000. The Canadian Legion has considered this matter very carefully and recommends that the permissible equity value of the house in which a recipient of war veterans allowance resides be increased from $6,000 to $9,000.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that deals with these recommendations. I have not taken time to elaborate on them. I do not think that is necessary. But I do ask the government on behalf of this group to give consideration to establishing a veterans affairs committee as soon as possible, and permitting the Legion and other organizations to present their evidence and their arguments before that committee. I am confident of this; that if the members of the committee recognize the validity of the evidence and the arguments, and appreciate the situation of many of the veterans in this country on whose behalf the Legion speaks, we shall have some very appropriate amendments to the Canadian Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
Before leaving this matter of veterans affairs I would like to refer briefly to the question of small holdings. In my opinion the most successful housing program undertaken by this government has been by the Department of Veterans Affairs under the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act. Unfortunately, as I have mentioned I think in eight previous years in this house, veterans are in many cases unable to take advantage of this excellent legislation because of the acreage requirements. I understand at least three acres of land are required to qualify if the land is not valued at $500 an acre or less, but that it is possible to obtain qualification in respect of 1.6 acres if the land is valued at $500 or more.
I know one veteran who has a piece of property just 1.56 acres in size. He does not qualify under the small holdings provision of the Veterans' Land Act. I do urge reconsideration of this acreage requirement

in order that we may meet the needs of veterans in many parts of Canada, particularly in British Columbia, where it is difficult to get these larger areas of land such as three acres and so on. In order that no veteran should be prevented from taking advantage of the act the acreage requirements in my opinion should be reduced to half an acre. In my own constituency there are nearly 400 veterans who are denied an opportunity to take advantage of the act by the present acreage requirements, men who would be able to take advantage of it if the requirement was reduced to half an acre. If the position is as serious as this in the constituency I have the honour to represent, similar circumstances must exist in many other ridings in Canada, and I urge the government to give consideration to this question.
Mr. Speaker, I just wish to make a few remarks with reference to international affairs. Since the house adjourned in August I have had the opportunity of visiting England, Belgium and France, and while there I took every opportunity to investigate the administration of the various departments of government; to discuss matters with labour people and industrialists; to visit housing developments in Britain and France, and to see many other interesting things.
I had the opportunity while in France of visiting all the Canadian fronts of the first world war. I have a particular and personal interest in those fronts, and while I was there I had occasion to see the Canadian war memorials now under the administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I have no hesitation in saying that the war memorial at Vimy is the finest war memorial in France or Belgium. It is magnificent in design, in conception and in location, and I must pay a tribute to the officials of the department and their gardener assistants in France for the excellent way in which the gardens are kept, for the landscaping, and the administration in general. The administration of war memorials in Belgium and France is a credit to the Canadian people.
In addition, I had the opportunity to look at some housing developments in France which I thought were very ugly indeed. I cannot understand how people like the French, who have developed such magnificent architecture in centuries past, can now be constructing such ugly and uninteresting housing developments. I saw development after development without any particular design at all, with houses like boxes, built of cement and ugly in the extreme, apparently

built with only one object in view, to house as many people as possible within a certain space.
I returned to England and had the opportunity to sit in the House of Commons during the major portion of the debate on the Suez issue. I must say that I received every courtesy from members of all parties and members of the House of Lords whom I had the opportunity to meet. I sat there and listened to that interesting debate, and I was particularly struck with one thing. I talked to members of the house, members of the upper house and other persons I met generally, and travelled around a great deal. What struck me particularly was the basic stability and underlying cohesion of the British people, regardless of the great division of opinion on a most serious and important matter; an underlying stability and cohesion that kept the nation, shall I say, united in principle although divided on a particular issue, an issue of such serious moment that it could have split apart other nations we know.
I was particularly pleased with the very high quality of the debate in the House of Commons and in the House of Lords, and I must say that as an Anglican I was delighted to hear the Archbishop of Canterbury say what he thought about the Suez issue. He was very vigorous in the expression of his opinion about that issue; he was chivied a bit afterwards by three or four noble lords who spoke after him, and he rose on three or four occasions to defend what he had said. But regardless of the deep division there is a tremendous respect for the elected representatives of the people in Great Britain and no one, whether they were on the government side of the benches or the Labour side, questioned anyone's motives. All that was questioned was the action that was undertaken.
I see that my time is disappearing very quickly and I must hurry along. I had the opportunity to go to the United Nations as a parliamentary observer. I think that is an excellent arrangement. Apparently ours is the only government that does it exactly in that way, and anyone who takes full advantage of the opportunity provided as a parliamentary observer at the United Nations must find it a fruitful and useful experience.
I must take this opportunity to compliment the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his work at the United Nations in recent months. It is recognized throughout the world, and Canada's prestige is particularly high at this time. I spoke to representatives of other nations, and whether they agree with us completely about this or that Canada is recognized as a country without any exterior
The Address-Mr. A. Gauthier ambitions, able to look upon these questions in a very objective manner. I have no hesitation in paying my tribute to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the magnificent job he has done in recent months.
However, having said that I find that there is some division in the Liberal party. This party is united on this issue. I find there is one section of the Liberal party that has what I would term a duplex, reversible international policy. I want to read a Canadian Press dispatch of November 9, 1956. The heading is, "Thatcher Lauds Eden's Actions", and it is in these words:
Ross Thatcher, member of parliament for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, says Prime Minister Sir Anthony Eden may have saved the Middle East from communism by moving forces into Egypt.
The former C.C.F. member, now Liberal candidate for Assiniboia in the next federal election, said Wednesday Eden "by halting the antics of a sawdust Hitler may well have saved the Middle East from communism.
"Canadians generally are proud of the part taken by Lester Pearson in the United Nations in bringing about a cease-fire. It is quite possible that in so doing he has prevented a third world war."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, custom and tradition have given a great flexibility to the debate on the address in reply. That is why I shall take this opportunity to express personal opinions on special problems, especially those of particular concern to the people I have the honour to represent in this house.
Before going into the main part of my remarks, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The well prepared speeches they have made reflect their knowledge of politics and of the problems of the day. Their constituents have reason to be proud of the choice they made at the last general election, a choice which they will no doubt renew with pleasure at the next election.
The agricultural class and the working class share about equally in the economic

The Address-Mr. A. Gauthier activity of the constituency of Lake St. John. Generally speaking we are quite happy about our lot. The Aluminum Company of Canada which, together with the pulp and paper industry, is responsible for the industrialization of the district, has just undertaken works of immense magnitude on the Peribonca river, in the northern part of the constituency, in order to develop hydroelectric power to the extent of 700,000 horsepower. 1,500 men are already gainfully employed there and it is assumed that before the end of the summer this figure will have more than doubled. Before that project is completed, lines of vats for the production of aluminum will be erected at He Maligne so that the production of aluminum ingots in this locality should be equal to that of Arvida which is at present the greatest aluminum producing centre. It means that the working class is justified in hoping for a high level of employment and for reasonable salaries but, even though full employment brings prosperity to all sections of our economy, the situation of the farmer remains unstable and unsatisfactory.
Agriculture is a section of our Canadian economy to which the government must give particular attention; I am glad to see that the speech from the throne provides greater encouragement for agriculture.
On January 9, in the course of this debate, the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has shown that he is well aware of the situation of our Quebec farmers and of the importance, to the Canadian economy, of our agricultural element. That is the reason why the Senate investigation proposed by the government cannot but bring beneficial results for agriculture as a whole as well as an improvement of economic conditions for our farmers.
Meanwhile, a good way to help the farmers, as well as the workers with large families, would be to increase the rate of family allowances.
We are indebted to the Right Honourable Mackenzie King and to the liberal party for this excellent social legislation. I do not know of any other social measure offering as many advantages as the Family Allowances Act; it is the one that helps the largest number of Canadians.
Since 1945, the cost of living has increased substantially, so that the original value of the allowances has sharply decreased.
We are now facing a serious threat of inflation, which causes more concern to those who come under a measure of such a high social value.
I have received requests from several hundreds of my constituents who are asking

the government to increase the rate of family allowances.
I support these requests, Mr. Speaker, for I know they are rightful requests. If the government could double those amounts it would be a very good thing, but the least that can be done is to give these social dividends the buying power they had in 1945.
Ever since I became a member of this house I have taken a keen interest in unemployment insurance. As a matter of fact, at the first session of the last parliament I asked that our bushworkers come under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I thought that the need for protection was greatest for those who are the most exposed to fluctuations in the labour market. That is why I did not hesitate to speak on their behalf in this house. And it was not in vain, since on April 1, 1950, bushworkers could qualify as all other workers.
When the law was revised, in 1955, I advocated the abrogation of the seasonal regulations concerning that class of workers. I wish to thank the authorities of the commission who saw fit to grant my request and the request which was made, the same day, by my colleague from Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais).
The purpose of the revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act was to extend its application to a larger number of people, and to increase the amount of the benefits. We have achieved our goal in part, but I thought I should make a suggestion to the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) in order to improve the lot of those who want to avail themselves of it to a larger extent.
Amendments to the act voted early last session had the effect of assimilating the rate of seasonal benefits to the rate of ordinary benefits and to extend to ten weeks the minimum period during which an unemployed person is entitled to receive such payments during the off season. When bringing in these amendments, the legislators had mainly in mind the human side of the question; this is why I too want to suggest that seasonal benefits should begin to be paid as from early December; a construction worker generally becomes unemployed at the end of November and such amendment as I just proposed would enable our unemployed to receive unemployment benefits before the Christmas and New Year holidays. What a comfort it would be to those people who are already in a plight after losing their jobs to receive benefits enabling them to buy at least the bare necessities of life at that time of the year!

Each of us still remembers with anxiety the events of last fall, when Israel, France and England, each in turn, invaded Egypt. Upon this occasion, our Prime Minister and our representatives in the United Nations played a most important part and history will recognize that Canada, in proposing the creation of an international police force, found the formula which prevented another world war. I must say that I was very proud of the firm attitude of our Prime Minister. His words and his deeds proved to the world that our country was an independent and sovereign country and that, consequently, it could take its own responsibilities and its own attitudes.
Afterwards, an incident occurred which emphasized a national weakness, namely the absence of a distinctive national flag. Hon. members will recall the refusal of Colonel Nasser to approve the presence of a Canadian battalion because the flag of that regiment contained a union jack which could lead to confusion with the British flag.
I have brought up this question of a flag two or three times in this house but, in view of its importance, I want to raise it again.
On December 9, 1953, seconding a motion introduced by my colleague from Bonaven-ture (Mr. Arsenault), I made the following statements which I would like to repeat today:
We have achieved national unity through the efforts of the Liberal party and of those who have been Its leaders for the past 50 years. It is also under Liberal administrations, and more particularly through the efforts of our present leaders, that our country progressed through the various stages that led to complete sovereignty and independence. The logical consequence of our previous moves would therefore be to endow our country with a distinctive national flag.
There has been much thought of national unity. To my mind there is nothing more important for the furtherance of that national unity than a flag which, in every circumstance, should serve as a rallying sign for all Canadians. Every citizen of this country is proud of belonging to this great Canadian nation of ours. The best way to give concrete form to this pride is to adopt an exclusive Canadian symbol.
Certain timorous individuals, more imperialistic than Canadian, fear that by doing away with the union jack we will weaken the ties that bind us to the commonwealth. To them I would say that the strength of the whole is the sum total of the strength of the parts. In any event these people should now understand that sentimental links are a thing of the past so far as Canada is concerned and that if we remain in the commonwealth it is because we find it to be in our interest, to begin with, as well as in the common interest of the free peoples and of the cause of world peace.
The present Prime Minister has stated on various occasions that he is favourable to the
The Address-Mr. Van Horne adoption of a truly distinctive flag, but he believes, wisely, in my opinion, that the taking of such a step must not be a matter for controversies sufficiently bitter to prejudice national unity.
Last Tuesday when the house opened, he said something which has given me an idea which I would like to pass on to the government. In congratulating the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. Prime Minister said:
I extend to the Leader of the Opposition our sincere good wishes in his new position and I wish to assure him quite seriously that I will be ready at all times to discuss with him in advance matters which need not be controversial on party lines and about which national unity might perhaps be best served by solutions that we could all recommend to those whom we represent in parliament.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the choice of a truly distinctive national flag should not be a controversial matter in Canada. That is why I am suggesting a conference of the four party leaders; if there are still some Canadians who do not favour a distinctive national flag, I say that the duty of the party leaders is to direct and guide public opinion.
Such a consultation would acquaint us with the opinion of the different party leaders and, I am sure, would bring about a unanimous feeling on a question so essential to Canadian sovereignty and to the independence of our beautiful and great country.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that the population has heard with the greatest satisfaction about the settlement of the Canadian Pacific strike.
I wish to congratulate the hon. Prime Minister for his part in the negotiations. He has shown that, in this field, as well as in many others, he is a true leader for the Canadian nation. I am sure that, when the time comes, Canada will show him its appreciation.

From that first day, the first day of confederation, the day on which so many of our forefathers flew the flag at half mast, our representatives of the maritimes, apart from those who were blinded and silenced by this trained seal, safe seat somewhere Liberal subservience, have risen and spoken for the maritimes.

Transportation in the maritime provinces is as much a stumbling block to progress as lack of power. We demand, as we have demanded over the years, drastic reductions in transportation rates to the full extent needed to permit competition by maritime producers and manufacturers in confederation-made markets. We demand action, and we demand it now. We demand a whole, new and complete revision of our freight rates act. In other words, we have demanded and we demand again a new deal for the maritime provinces.
Power has long held us up. Even today the pulp mill at Dalhousie is held up for lack of power. Every day opportunities to develop our mines are lost because of lack

of power. Let us look at what this government did and what it is doing regarding the position at Beeehwood. Lack of capital for our industrial development has also held us up for a long time, and don't think for one minute that the industrial development bank does more than render lip service in the maritime provinces. Surely when New Brunswick asked the government for the endorsement of its note we were not asking for a hand-out. The Address-Mr. Van Horne

With this as the objective it is suggested that the people of Canada as a whole may be willing to assist the people of the Atlantic provinces in discovering, developing and making the best use of resources in that area.

Every year that passes, no matter how we strive, no matter what risks we take or what gambles we risk-every year that passes leaves us relatively weaker compared with the rest of Canada.
How long can this go on? The people will be sucked irresistibly into richer and more attractive parts of Canada. We are not willing to lie down and die on the Atlantic coast. We shall kick up such a devil of a row that we shall make them ashamed.
He added some hopeful words at that time. Premier Smallwood prophesied that the Gordon commission would produce a new charter for the Atlantic provinces and that confederation would begin to mean just and equal treatment for the Atlantic provinces.
There was the prophecy and the Gordon report is the reality. As one of the newspapers said, "We say thank you very much, Mr. Gordon-thank you for nothing; we knew all about it before you said those things".
Mr. Speaker, I see my time is about up. There are a few more subjects I would like to discuss. I have not approached the subject of unemployment insurance, which in my riding and in many sections of this country continues to be one horrible mess. We see big families whose fathers work at seasonal jobs, jobs that do not give them the required number of stamps, and I have visited families in distress because of this; I have seen them time and time again. I have brought hon. members of this house to visit families where there were no fires in the house and where an orange crate was used as a cupboard, often with very little in it and sometimes nothing at all, simply because these people lacked two weeks of stamps. They have to eke out a living as best they can, simply because this government has refused to give them unemployment insurance benefits. Why call it unemployment insurance if it is not going to be that?
It is not the fault of these people. I speak today for the suffering people of this country of whom this government is not aware, judging by its actions and especially with regard

The Address-Mr. Van Horne to unemployment insurance. I am sorry the Minister of Labour is not here in his place tonight, because I have a few things to say when he is here and I will wait until he comes into the house before saying them.

There can be no doubt in anyone's mind that the people of the country expect more of the unemployment insurance commission than it is doing with over $950 million in reserve. Surely methods can be adopted to reduce the number of weeks required to obtain unemployment insurance. What possible reason can you give? I look across the floor at this baby sitter, the hon. member for Gloucester, and I know full well the conditions that exist in his riding, and how the people are suffering. I ask, "Why are you hoarding this money?" Why is the government not taking steps?
